family-fam-01.title: Your bank says: move it now
family-fam-01.prompt: A text claiming to be your bank says a $2,400 transfer is pending. A caller follows seconds later, knows your name, and says you must move your balance to a “protected account” before the transfer settles.
family-fam-01.answersA: Hang up and contact the bank through the number in its app or on your card; do not move money on an incoming caller’s instructions.
family-fam-01.answersB: Freeze the card/account in the bank app first, then contact the bank through a known channel.
family-fam-01.answersC: Move only part of the money to the protected account while you verify the rest.
family-fam-01.explanation: Real fraud teams may act urgently, but they do not need you to transfer your own money to make it safe.
family-fam-01.proTip: A “safe account” controlled by the caller is not safe.

family-fam-02.title: Power off in 45 minutes
family-fam-02.prompt: A caller says your electricity account is overdue and service will be disconnected in 45 minutes. The amount sounds plausible, and they offer to “hold the shutoff” if you pay immediately by card.
family-fam-02.answersA: Ask for the account number and overdue amount, then compare them with your own bill before doing anything.
family-fam-02.answersB: Pay the amount if it matches your normal monthly bill, then dispute it later if necessary.
family-fam-02.answersC: End the call and check your utility account or call the number on a bill or official site.
family-fam-02.explanation: Urgency plus a believable amount can create false confidence. Verify the debt independently before paying.
family-fam-02.proTip: A familiar bill amount is not proof of a familiar caller.

family-fam-03.title: Field trip closes tonight
family-fam-03.prompt: A message in a parent chat says the school’s field-trip payment portal is down and shares a new payment link that expires tonight. Several parents react with thumbs-up emojis.
family-fam-03.answersA: Pay because other parents appear to be using it and the deadline is real.
family-fam-03.answersB: Use the school portal or a known school contact to confirm the payment method before paying.
family-fam-03.answersC: Ask the chat admin or another parent you know personally whether the school announced a new link.
family-fam-03.explanation: Group-chat momentum can make a fake link feel community-approved. The school’s own channel should confirm any payment change.
family-fam-03.proTip: Crowd confidence is not payment verification.

family-fam-04.title: Your package needs $1.72
family-fam-04.prompt: You are expecting a package when a text says delivery failed because your address is incomplete. It asks for $1.72 to schedule redelivery and shows a tracking number that looks plausible.
family-fam-04.answersA: Open the retailer or carrier app/site you already use and check the tracking number there.
family-fam-04.answersB: Search the carrier independently and contact support with the tracking number.
family-fam-04.answersC: Pay the small fee because you are expecting a delivery and the amount is too small to be worth scamming.
family-fam-04.explanation: Tiny fees are useful bait for collecting card and identity data. Expected deliveries make the story more believable, not more verified.
family-fam-04.proTip: Small charge, potentially big data loss.

family-fam-05.title: The toll doubles tomorrow
family-fam-05.prompt: A text says you owe $6.40 in unpaid tolls and warns the fee becomes $75 tomorrow and may affect vehicle registration. You drove on toll roads last week.
family-fam-05.answersA: Call the toll agency using a known number and ask them to search your plate/account.
family-fam-05.answersB: Pay through the text link because the amount is plausible and you did use toll roads.
family-fam-05.answersC: Use your toll account or the toll agency website you navigate to independently to check for an actual balance.
family-fam-05.explanation: Real-world context makes toll smishing effective. The toll authority can verify debt without using the text link.
family-fam-05.proTip: Recent driving makes the story plausible, not authenticated.

family-fam-06.title: Refund expires at midnight
family-fam-06.prompt: An email says a tax refund adjustment is waiting but must be claimed before midnight. The page asks you to confirm bank details and a government ID number.
family-fam-06.answersA: Enter the bank details now but leave the ID field blank until the refund status updates.
family-fam-06.answersB: Ignore the link and check your tax account or tax authority through its official site and normal communication process.
family-fam-06.answersC: Ask your tax preparer or accountant whether such a refund process is legitimate.
family-fam-06.explanation: Refund urgency is designed to turn good news into rushed disclosure. Tax authorities have established channels for account changes.
family-fam-06.proTip: Unexpected money deserves the same skepticism as unexpected debt.

family-fam-07.title: Your computer has “4 minutes to quarantine”
family-fam-07.prompt: A browser warning fills the screen and plays an alarm. It says your photos are being encrypted and gives a support number to call before a four-minute quarantine countdown reaches zero.
family-fam-07.answersA: Do not call the number; close the browser if possible and use your device’s trusted security tools or a known support provider.
family-fam-07.answersB: Disconnect from the internet and ask a trusted person or support provider to inspect the device.
family-fam-07.answersC: Call the displayed number but refuse to install anything until they prove they are legitimate.
family-fam-07.explanation: Scare screens use urgency to make the attacker the only apparent helper. The support channel shown by the warning is part of the warning.
family-fam-07.proTip: The alarm is part of the persuasion.

family-fam-08.title: Tonight’s show, “instant refund”
family-fam-08.prompt: A ticket marketplace message says your event was cancelled and offers an instant refund if you confirm the payment card within 30 minutes. You already saw social posts saying the event may be cancelled.
family-fam-08.answersA: Contact the venue or marketplace using a known channel and ask what refund process applies.
family-fam-08.answersB: Use the message link because independent social posts make the cancellation credible.
family-fam-08.answersC: Open the ticketing account/app yourself and check the event and refund status there.
family-fam-08.explanation: A real cancellation can be exploited by scammers immediately. Verify the refund path, not just the event news.
family-fam-08.proTip: True event, false refund link is still a scam.

family-fam-09.title: Your claim payout “closes today”
family-fam-09.prompt: After a recent home claim, a caller says your insurer approved a payout but needs updated bank details before the file closes at 5 p.m. They know the claim type and approximate amount.
family-fam-09.answersA: Provide the bank details because the caller knows information only the insurer should know.
family-fam-09.answersB: End the call and check the claim in the insurer app/site or call the number on your policy.
family-fam-09.answersC: Ask the caller to leave a note on the claim, then verify the request through your account.
family-fam-09.explanation: Claim information can leak through documents, emails, or vendors. Payment-destination changes need independent verification.
family-fam-09.proTip: Claim knowledge is not caller authentication.

family-fam-10.title: Pay today, save 35%
family-fam-10.prompt: A caller says an old medical balance was sent to collections but can be closed today for 35% less. They know the provider name and date of service and offer a payment link by text.
family-fam-10.answersA: Contact the provider or collector through independently verified contact details and request written validation before paying.
family-fam-10.answersB: Check your insurance explanation of benefits and provider portal to see whether the balance exists.
family-fam-10.answersC: Pay the discounted amount now because the details match a real visit and the deal may disappear.
family-fam-10.explanation: Real medical details can be combined with fake collection pressure. Verify who owns the debt before settling it.
family-fam-10.proTip: A discount is not a substitute for debt validation.

family-fam-11.title: Caller ID says your bank
family-fam-11.prompt: Your phone displays your bank’s name. The caller says a new device is trying to access your account and asks you to read back the six-digit code that just arrived by text.
family-fam-11.answersA: Freeze sensitive transactions in the app, then call the bank yourself.
family-fam-11.answersB: Read the code because it arrived from the bank’s normal text number and the caller ID matches.
family-fam-11.answersC: Do not read the code; hang up and contact the bank through its app or the number on your card.
family-fam-11.explanation: Caller ID can be spoofed, and one-time codes often authorize access. The bank should not need you to relay a code to an incoming caller.
family-fam-11.proTip: A code that proves you are you should stay with you.

family-fam-12.title: There is a warrant—pay by kiosk
family-fam-12.prompt: A caller claiming to be law enforcement says you missed a court notice and a warrant can be paused if you pay a bond today. They instruct you to stay on the line while withdrawing cash.
family-fam-12.answersA: Follow the instructions until you reach the payment step, then verify before sending anything.
family-fam-12.answersB: End the call and contact the court or police agency through official published numbers; do not pay on the caller’s instructions.
family-fam-12.answersC: Write down the officer name, badge number and case number, then verify them independently.
family-fam-12.explanation: Threats and official-sounding details are designed to keep you compliant and isolated. Real agencies can be contacted independently.

family-fam-13.title: The principal wants gift cards
family-fam-13.prompt: An email from the principal’s display name asks you to buy gift cards for student awards before a meeting. It says the school will reimburse you and asks for the card numbers by reply.
family-fam-13.answersA: Verify the request with the principal or school office through a known channel before purchasing anything.
family-fam-13.answersB: Ask the sender to submit the request through the school’s normal purchasing process.
family-fam-13.answersC: Buy the cards but keep the codes until the principal confirms in person.
family-fam-13.explanation: Authority and a helpful mission can bypass skepticism. Normal procurement controls are the stronger signal.
family-fam-13.proTip: Urgent generosity still needs normal controls.

family-fam-14.title: Your doctor needs your insurance login
family-fam-14.prompt: A caller says they are from your clinic’s billing team and a rejected claim can be fixed if you confirm your insurance portal login. They correctly name your doctor and recent appointment.
family-fam-14.answersA: Offer to provide the insurance member ID through the clinic’s secure portal instead of sharing a login.
family-fam-14.answersB: Share the login if the caller can confirm your appointment details.
family-fam-14.answersC: End the call and use the clinic portal or known clinic number to ask what information is actually needed.
family-fam-14.explanation: A clinic may need insurance information, but it should not need your insurer password. Familiar medical context can be stolen or guessed.
family-fam-14.proTip: Organizations may need account data; they do not need your account password.

family-fam-15.title: The closing instructions changed
family-fam-15.prompt: The day before a home purchase closes, an email that looks like it came from the title company says its receiving bank changed after a “security upgrade.” It includes new wire instructions and warns that late funds could delay the keys.
family-fam-15.answersA: Use the new instructions because the email has the correct property address, closing amount and staff signature.
family-fam-15.answersB: Call the title company or closing attorney using a number from earlier paperwork—not the email—and verbally verify the account details before sending anything.
family-fam-15.answersC: Pause the transfer and ask for the bank change to be confirmed through the established closing portal or in person.
family-fam-15.explanation: Real-estate wire fraud often relies on compromised email and accurate transaction details. A changed payment destination deserves independent verbal verification.
family-fam-15.proTip: For large wires, verify the destination using a contact method established before the change.

family-fam-16.title: The tax agency wants “verification”
family-fam-16.prompt: A letter-looking email says your identity must be verified before your tax return can be processed. It links to a page asking for a selfie, ID and full bank account number.
family-fam-16.answersA: Go to the tax authority’s official site yourself and check whether an identity-verification notice exists in your account.
family-fam-16.answersB: Call the tax authority using a published number and ask what documents are legitimately required.
family-fam-16.answersC: Upload the ID and selfie first but wait to enter the bank details until you receive confirmation.
family-fam-16.explanation: Government identity checks can be real, which is why the channel matters. Verify the notice before sending a complete identity bundle.
family-fam-16.proTip: Sensitive documents belong in a verified government process, not an email link.

family-fam-17.title: Jury duty “failure to appear”
family-fam-17.prompt: A caller says you failed to appear for jury duty and must pay a civil fine before a judge reviews the case. They know your address and local courthouse name.
family-fam-17.answersA: Ask for the case number and judge name, then verify them independently.
family-fam-17.answersB: Pay if the caller accepts a normal credit card and provides a receipt rather than gift cards or crypto.
family-fam-17.answersC: Hang up and contact the court using its official website or published clerk number.
family-fam-17.explanation: Professional payment methods do not authenticate a government demand. The court itself can confirm whether the case exists.
family-fam-17.proTip: Normal payment method, abnormal process: still verify.

family-fam-18.title: Your pension account is “frozen”
family-fam-18.prompt: A caller claiming to be from a benefits agency says unusual activity froze your pension account. They ask you to confirm your identity by reading a code sent to your phone.
family-fam-18.answersA: Read the code because the agency already has your phone number and sent it to you.
family-fam-18.answersB: End the call and sign in through the official benefits portal or call the agency using a known number.
family-fam-18.answersC: Ask the caller to send a notice to your online account, then verify it there.
family-fam-18.explanation: One-time codes are frequently used to take over accounts. An incoming caller should not need the credential that unlocks your account.
family-fam-18.proTip: If the caller needs your login code, they may be trying to become you.

family-fam-19.title: Property management changed banks
family-fam-19.prompt: An email from your property manager says the rent collection account changed after a banking merger. It includes the building address and manager signature and asks you to update the standing order.
family-fam-19.answersA: Verify the new bank details with the property manager through a known phone number or tenant portal before changing payment instructions.
family-fam-19.answersB: Ask for the change to appear in the official tenant portal or formal lease communication.
family-fam-19.answersC: Make one small test transfer to the new account before moving the full rent payment.
family-fam-19.explanation: Small test payments only prove the account receives money, not that it belongs to your landlord. Bank-detail changes require identity verification.

family-fam-20.title: Carrier support can “save your number”
family-fam-20.prompt: A caller claiming to be your mobile carrier says someone requested a SIM transfer. They can cancel it if you tell them the security PIN sent by text within five minutes.
family-fam-20.answersA: Log in yourself and change the account PIN/password before contacting support.
family-fam-20.answersB: Read the PIN because preventing a SIM swap is time-sensitive and the caller is offering to stop it.
family-fam-20.answersC: End the call and contact the carrier through its official app, site or known support number to secure the account.
family-fam-20.explanation: The code may be exactly what an attacker needs to complete a SIM swap. Secure the account from a channel you control.
family-fam-20.proTip: Do not hand the “stop the attack” caller the code that completes the attack.

family-fam-21.title: Mom, I need you—don’t tell Dad
family-fam-21.prompt: You get a call that sounds like your adult child. They say they caused an accident, are embarrassed, and need money sent to a lawyer immediately. They beg you not to call anyone else.
family-fam-21.answersA: Send a small amount first so they can prove they received it before you send the rest.
family-fam-21.answersB: End the call and contact your child through a known number or verify through another trusted family member or family code word.
family-fam-21.answersC: Keep the caller talking while another family member independently contacts your child.
family-fam-21.explanation: Voice cloning and emotional isolation are powerful together. Independent family contact is the fastest way to break the script.
family-fam-21.proTip: “Do not tell anyone” is exactly when you should tell someone.

family-fam-22.title: The grandson with a broken phone
family-fam-22.prompt: A message from a new number says, “Hi Grandma, dropped my phone in water. This is my temporary number.” The conversation sounds natural and soon asks for help paying an urgent car-repair bill.
family-fam-22.answersA: Call your grandchild on the old number or contact another family member before sending money.
family-fam-22.answersB: Ask a personal question only your grandchild should know, then verify through a second channel.
family-fam-22.answersC: Send the money if the answer to your personal question is correct.
family-fam-22.explanation: Personal facts can be learned from social media or prior breaches. A second channel is stronger than trivia-based identity checks.
family-fam-22.proTip: Family facts are clues, not authentication.

family-fam-23.title: Dad has a “new number”
family-fam-23.prompt: A familiar profile photo appears on WhatsApp from a new number: “Old phone died. Please delete the old contact.” An hour later, “Dad” asks you to pay an invoice because his banking app is still locked.
family-fam-23.answersA: Ask for a voice or video call and verify something current before trusting the new number.
family-fam-23.answersB: Pay if the invoice is for a company or bill you recognize.
family-fam-23.answersC: Call your father on a known number or verify with another family member before changing the contact or paying anything.
family-fam-23.explanation: Recognizing the bill does not authenticate the person asking you to pay it. New numbers deserve independent confirmation.
family-fam-23.proTip: New number + money request = verify the person first.

family-fam-24.title: A relationship becomes an investment club
family-fam-24.prompt: Someone you met online has talked with you daily for two months. They never pressured you for money, but now they offer to teach you a trading strategy and show screenshots of strong returns.
family-fam-24.answersA: Try a very small investment and only continue if you can withdraw it.
family-fam-24.answersB: Do not invest through a platform or wallet recommended by an online romantic interest; keep the relationship and money separate.
family-fam-24.answersC: Research the platform independently and discuss the idea with a trusted financial professional or friend before acting.
family-fam-24.explanation: Long-con romance investment scams build trust first and may allow early withdrawals to increase confidence.
family-fam-24.proTip: Time invested in a relationship is not due diligence on an investment.

family-fam-25.title: Your friend sends a “vote for me” link
family-fam-25.prompt: A friend’s Instagram account asks you to vote for them in a contest. The link opens a login page and they message, “Please hurry—voting closes soon.” The conversation style sounds like them.
family-fam-25.answersA: Contact your friend through another channel and do not enter credentials into the contest link.
family-fam-25.answersB: Open the contest site independently and see whether your friend is actually listed.
family-fam-25.answersC: Log in if your password manager recognizes the page and autofills your credentials.
family-fam-25.explanation: Compromised accounts inherit the victim’s real history and tone. Cross-channel verification checks whether your friend still controls the account.
family-fam-25.proTip: A familiar account can be an unfamiliar operator.

family-fam-26.title: Your neighbor wants a deposit
family-fam-26.prompt: Someone in a neighborhood group offers a high-end stroller at a very good price. Their profile has local posts going back years, and they ask for a deposit because “three other people are interested.”
family-fam-26.answersA: Message through the platform and check whether the seller will provide a current photo with a specific detail you request.
family-fam-26.answersB: Send a small deposit because the long-standing local profile makes fraud unlikely.
family-fam-26.answersC: Arrange an in-person pickup/payment or use a marketplace payment method with buyer protection.
family-fam-26.explanation: Established social accounts can be compromised. Transaction protections matter more than profile age.
family-fam-26.proTip: Old profile, new seller: protect the transaction.

family-fam-27.title: The family fundraiser in your group chat
family-fam-27.prompt: A relative shares a fundraiser link for a family in your community after a house fire. The story is real and local news confirms the fire, but the donation page is hosted on an unfamiliar site.
family-fam-27.answersA: Donate because the underlying emergency is confirmed by local news.
family-fam-27.answersB: Verify the fundraiser through the affected family, a known organizer, or a recognized fundraising platform before donating.
family-fam-27.answersC: Donate directly to a verified local organization helping the family instead of using the shared link.
family-fam-27.explanation: Real tragedies are often reused in fake fundraising pages. Verify where the money goes, not only whether the event happened.
family-fam-27.proTip: True story, false collection page is still fraud.

family-fam-28.title: The new caregiver asks for account access
family-fam-28.prompt: A caregiver helping an older relative says the pharmacy portal keeps rejecting the refill. They ask for the relative’s email password so they can “sort it out while they are here.”
family-fam-28.answersA: Keep the password private and use delegated access, a pharmacy call, or sit with the relative while they log in themselves.
family-fam-28.answersB: Reset the pharmacy account and create a separate access method if the service supports it.
family-fam-28.answersC: Share the password temporarily, then change it after the refill is complete.
family-fam-28.explanation: A legitimate helper may have a legitimate need, but shared master credentials create unnecessary risk and confusion later.
family-fam-28.proTip: Help should get the least access needed to help.

family-fam-29.title: Your cousin is stranded overseas
family-fam-29.prompt: A cousin’s social account messages that their wallet was stolen while traveling. They send a photo of a police report and ask you to wire money to the hotel manager because their own account is blocked.
family-fam-29.answersA: Call the hotel using a number you find independently and ask whether the person is actually staying there.
family-fam-29.answersB: Send money because the police report and hotel details make the story credible.
family-fam-29.answersC: Contact your cousin through another known channel or family member and verify the emergency before sending anything.
family-fam-29.explanation: Documents can be forged and hacked accounts carry real personal history. Verify the person outside the compromised channel.
family-fam-29.proTip: Documents support a story; they do not authenticate the storyteller.

family-fam-30.title: The pet rescue knows your dog
family-fam-30.prompt: A local rescue account messages after you post that your dog is missing. They say a volunteer found a matching dog and ask for a small “scanner and transport fee” before sharing the location.
family-fam-30.answersA: Pay the small fee because the rescue account knows your dog’s name and description.
family-fam-30.answersB: Ask for verifiable evidence such as a live video or identifying detail, and contact the rescue through its official published channel before paying.
family-fam-30.answersC: Meet at a safe public location or animal shelter without paying a release fee first.
family-fam-30.explanation: Public lost-pet posts give scammers everything needed to sound specific. Verification should involve the animal, not just the post details.
family-fam-30.proTip: Information from your post is not secret proof.

family-fam-31.title: Support wants to “see the problem”
family-fam-31.prompt: A caller claiming to be from your bank says malware may be causing suspicious transfers. They ask you to install a remote-support app so they can inspect your phone while you log in.
family-fam-31.answersA: Do not install the app; end the call and contact the bank through its official channel, then secure the device separately if needed.
family-fam-31.answersB: Use the bank app to freeze transactions first and ask a trusted tech-support provider to inspect the device.
family-fam-31.answersC: Install the app but close your banking app before giving them screen access.
family-fam-31.explanation: Remote-control tools can expose passwords, messages and approvals even if the banking app is closed.
family-fam-31.proTip: If the helper needs control of your screen, verify the helper first.

family-fam-32.title: “Read me the code to cancel it”
family-fam-32.prompt: A caller says someone is resetting your email password. A six-digit code arrives, and the caller asks you to read it aloud so they can cancel the reset.
family-fam-32.answersA: Change the password and review active sessions before contacting support.
family-fam-32.answersB: Share the code because the caller is using it to cancel, not approve, the reset.
family-fam-32.answersC: Do not share the code; end the call and secure the email account from the official app/site.
family-fam-32.explanation: The same code can often complete the reset the caller claims to be stopping.
family-fam-32.proTip: Never let an incoming caller narrate what your security code “means.”

family-fam-33.title: A mystery package and a QR card
family-fam-33.prompt: A package you never ordered arrives with a note: “Scan to see who sent your gift.” The QR code opens a page asking you to sign in with your email before revealing the sender.
family-fam-33.answersA: Sign in if the package label has your correct name and address, since that proves the sender had your details.
family-fam-33.answersB: Do not sign in; verify the package through the retailer/carrier if possible and treat the QR code as untrusted.
family-fam-33.answersC: Scan only with a security-aware camera/browser and inspect the destination without entering any credentials.
family-fam-33.explanation: Unsolicited packages can be used to lure recipients into malicious QR flows. Your address may already be public or breached.
family-fam-33.proTip: A package can be physical bait for a digital trap.

family-fam-34.title: The TV asks for a pairing code
family-fam-34.prompt: A pop-up on your smart TV says your streaming session expired and shows a QR code to “re-pair this device.” The page on your phone asks for your email password and a recovery code.
family-fam-34.answersA: Close the prompt and pair the TV only through the streaming service’s official app/device settings.
family-fam-34.answersB: Restart the TV/app and check whether it still requests pairing through the normal flow.
family-fam-34.answersC: Enter the password but withhold the recovery code unless the TV confirms the pairing.
family-fam-34.explanation: Pairing should not require handing a recovery credential to an unfamiliar web page.
family-fam-34.proTip: Pair devices from the account you trust, not the pop-up you did not request.

family-fam-35.title: A family member needs your reset link
family-fam-35.prompt: Your partner says they are locked out of a shared household account and asks you to forward the password-reset email so they can finish the reset on their phone.
family-fam-35.answersA: Use the service’s family/delegated access if available instead of sharing reset tokens.
family-fam-35.answersB: Forward the reset link because you trust your partner and the account is shared anyway.
family-fam-35.answersC: Do not forward the reset link; initiate the reset together and update the password through the official account settings.
family-fam-35.explanation: Reset links are temporary master keys and can be abused if the partner’s device or message account is compromised.
family-fam-35.proTip: Trust the person; still protect the credential.

family-fam-36.title: The “safe account” transfer
family-fam-36.prompt: A bank impersonator convinces you that criminals are inside your account and says the only way to stop them is to transfer the balance to a temporary account at another bank “owned by the fraud department.”
family-fam-36.answersA: Transfer a small test amount first and wait for the caller to confirm it landed in the protected account.
family-fam-36.answersB: Do not transfer; end the call and contact your bank independently to freeze or secure the account.
family-fam-36.answersC: Lock cards and outgoing transfers in the bank app while you contact the bank yourself.
family-fam-36.explanation: Banks secure accounts internally; they do not protect your money by having you send it to a stranger-controlled account.
family-fam-36.proTip: Security does not require surrendering control of the money.

family-fam-37.title: The code is the payment
family-fam-37.prompt: Someone claiming to be a relative’s attorney says court fees must be paid immediately but their office cannot take cards after hours. They ask you to buy gift cards and send photos of the codes.
family-fam-37.answersA: Stop and verify the relative and the attorney independently; do not send gift-card codes as payment.
family-fam-37.answersB: Call the law office using a number you find independently and ask whether any fee is due.
family-fam-37.answersC: Buy the cards but keep the codes until you reach the relative directly.
family-fam-37.explanation: Gift-card codes function like cash once shared. The unusual payment method is itself a strong warning signal.
family-fam-37.proTip: If the “payment” is a code, treat it like cash leaving your hand.

family-fam-38.title: The officer sends a QR code
family-fam-38.prompt: A caller claiming to be from law enforcement says your identity was used in a financial crime. They tell you to withdraw cash, go to a crypto ATM and scan a QR code to place the money in “federal protection.”
family-fam-38.answersA: Speak with your bank before making any unusual cash withdrawal and explain the caller’s story.
family-fam-38.answersB: Deposit only a small amount first while you verify the case number.
family-fam-38.answersC: End the call and contact the agency through an official published number; do not use the ATM or QR code.
family-fam-38.explanation: Government agencies do not secure money by routing it through a crypto wallet controlled by a caller.
family-fam-38.proTip: A QR code at a crypto ATM is a destination address, not government protection.

family-fam-39.title: “Upload ID to unlock your account”
family-fam-39.prompt: A message says your shopping account is temporarily locked and asks you to upload a photo of your driver’s licence plus a selfie to restore access. The link opens a page that looks identical to the retailer.
family-fam-39.answersA: Upload the selfie first but wait to send the licence until the account status changes.
family-fam-39.answersB: Open the retailer app/site yourself and use its account-recovery process or support channel.
family-fam-39.answersC: Check whether the account is actually locked by signing in independently before providing any documents.
family-fam-39.explanation: A convincing page can collect an identity bundle for future fraud. First prove the account problem exists.
family-fam-39.proTip: Verify the problem before proving your identity.

family-fam-40.title: The buyer “overpaid” you
family-fam-40.prompt: You sell a sofa online. The buyer sends a payment screenshot showing they accidentally paid $300 extra and asks you to refund the difference immediately to a different payment handle.
family-fam-40.answersA: Check your actual account balance and transaction status; do not refund money that has not genuinely settled.
family-fam-40.answersB: Tell the buyer to cancel or reverse the payment through the platform/payment provider instead of sending a separate refund.
family-fam-40.answersC: Refund the difference once the screenshot shows a completed transaction, because keeping it would be unfair.
family-fam-40.explanation: Screenshots can be fabricated and some payments can later reverse. Never send a separate payment based only on an image.

family-fam-41.title: Amazon says: $749 charge pending
family-fam-41.prompt: A text and a follow-up call claim a $749 order just went through on your Amazon account. The message gives a phone number to call immediately to cancel before it ships.
family-fam-41.answersA: Open the Amazon app yourself and check your orders; call Amazon only through the number in the app if anything looks wrong.
family-fam-41.answersB: Call the number in the text to cancel the order before it ships.
family-fam-41.answersC: Stay on the line and read back the verification code they send to your phone.
family-fam-41.explanation: Real order alerts don't need you to call an unfamiliar number to cancel. The call is the scam - it moves you from a text into a live agent who asks for account access.
family-fam-41.proTip: Check orders inside the app you already trust, not through a number a message gives you.

family-fam-42.title: Your car warranty expires today
family-fam-42.prompt: A robocall says your vehicle's extended warranty expires today and a representative can lock in your current rate if you press 1 now.
family-fam-42.answersA: Press 1 and give your VIN and payment details to lock in the rate.
family-fam-42.answersB: Hang up. If your car actually has a warranty, it's with the dealer or manufacturer, and you can check without this call.
family-fam-42.answersC: Ask the caller to send an email first, then decide later.
family-fam-42.explanation: Extended-warranty robocalls are a decades-old numbers game - they call this exact line to everyone, whether or not you own a car with an active warranty.
family-fam-42.proTip: A real warranty renewal doesn't need to be locked in during a cold call.

family-fam-43.title: A debt from 2019 - court date Monday
family-fam-43.prompt: A caller says they represent a collections agency chasing an unpaid $1,240 debt from 2019. They say a court filing goes through Monday unless you settle today by card over the phone.
family-fam-43.answersA: Pay a smaller amount today to make the court filing stop.
family-fam-43.answersB: Ask for the collector's name, company, and a written notice, then verify independently before paying anything.
family-fam-43.answersC: Give your card number now to avoid the court filing.
family-fam-43.explanation: Legitimate debt collectors are required to send written validation of a debt on request, and real court processes don't resolve with a same-day card payment over the phone.
family-fam-43.proTip: A real debt survives a request for it in writing. A fake one doesn't.

family-fam-44.title: The bank is sending a courier for your card
family-fam-44.prompt: Someone calling from your bank's 'fraud team' says your card has been compromised. To protect you, they're sending a courier to collect the physical card within the hour, along with the PIN written on paper.
family-fam-44.answersA: Hand the card to the courier but keep the PIN only in your head.
family-fam-44.answersB: Hand over the card and PIN as instructed to stop the fraud.
family-fam-44.answersC: Hang up and call your bank using the number on the back of the card; banks never collect cards or PINs by courier.
family-fam-44.explanation: No legitimate bank ever sends someone to your door to collect your card or PIN. This is courier fraud, and it moves fast precisely so you don't have time to check.
family-fam-44.proTip: A bank protects a compromised card by freezing it - never by sending someone to collect it.

family-fam-45.title: Grandma, it's me - I'm in hospital
family-fam-45.prompt: A voice that sounds exactly like your grandson calls, crying, saying he was in an accident and needs money for a hospital deposit before they'll treat him. He begs you not to call his parents.
family-fam-45.answersA: Ask him a question only the real grandson would know, then decide what to do.
family-fam-45.answersB: Wire the deposit right away since he sounds so upset.
family-fam-45.answersC: Hang up and call your grandson or his parents directly on a number you already have.
family-fam-45.explanation: AI voice cloning can now copy a familiar voice from a few seconds of audio. A voice matching isn't proof of identity anymore - a callback on a known number is.
family-fam-45.proTip: The voice can be faked. The number you already have for them can't.

family-fam-46.title: Is this you in this video?
family-fam-46.prompt: A friend messages you a link asking, 'is this you in this video??' The message came from their real account, and you weren't expecting it.
family-fam-46.answersA: Click the link since it's from someone you know.
family-fam-46.answersB: Don't click. Message your friend a different way to ask if their account was hacked.
family-fam-46.answersC: Forward it to other friends to warn them, clicking through first to check.
family-fam-46.explanation: This is one of the most common hacked-account chains on social media - a compromised friend's account sends the same curiosity-bait link to their whole list.
family-fam-46.proTip: A familiar sender doesn't make a surprise link safe - check with them another way first.

family-fam-47.title: A mystery QR code on the parking meter
family-fam-47.prompt: The parking meter has an 'Out of Order - Scan to Pay' sticker with a QR code. Scanning it opens a payment page asking for your card number, expiry date, and CVV.
family-fam-47.answersA: Skip the QR code and pay through the official parking app or the meter's card reader instead.
family-fam-47.answersB: Scan it, but only enter the last four digits of your card.
family-fam-47.answersC: Scan it and pay - it's faster than finding the app.
family-fam-47.explanation: Fraudulent QR stickers placed over real parking signage are a fast-growing scam. The 'out of order' framing exists to push you toward the fake link instead of the official option.
family-fam-47.proTip: A sticker QR code on public equipment is never the safest way to pay - use the app or the machine itself.

family-fam-48.title: We refunded you $9,000 by mistake
family-fam-48.prompt: After a support call about a $90 refund, your account shows a $9,000 deposit. The 'agent' stays on the line, apologizes for the error, and asks you to wire back the difference immediately before their system flags it.
family-fam-48.answersA: Wire back the difference right away to fix their mistake.
family-fam-48.answersB: Wire back more than asked, to be safe, then request the rest back later.
family-fam-48.answersC: Hang up and check your real account balance and statement later; a support agent can never make your bank account show a fake deposit.
family-fam-48.explanation: The 'accidental overpayment' is a doctored screen or a temporary hold, not real money. Once you wire funds back, the fake deposit disappears and the money you sent is gone for good.
family-fam-48.proTip: If a refund suddenly requires you to send money, the refund isn't real.

family-family-red-flag-relay-FAM-W1.title: Family Red-Flag Relay
family-family-red-flag-relay-FAM-W1.prompt: Family online play: each player has 20 seconds to name one niche red flag from the last Family card without repeating another player.
family-family-red-flag-relay-FAM-W1.answersA: Complete the relay with no repeats.
family-family-red-flag-relay-FAM-W1.explanation: Family Red-Flag Relay: the purpose is to turn the last scenario into active recall, not passive reading. It rewards naming a precise safer action instead of giving vague advice.
family-family-red-flag-relay-FAM-W1.proTip: Use it only after a scenario card, never as a separate mini-game.

family-family-safer-channel-switch-FAM-W.title: Family Safer-Channel Switch
family-family-safer-channel-switch-FAM-W.prompt: Family online play: replace the risky channel in the last Family card with the safest niche verification channel.
family-family-safer-channel-switch-FAM-W.explanation: Family Safer-Channel Switch: the purpose is to turn the last scenario into active recall, not passive reading. It rewards naming a precise safer action instead of giving vague advice.
family-family-safer-channel-switch-FAM-W.proTip: Good answers name the exact channel: portal, app, saved number, official office, manager, IT, provider, or platform.

school-sch-01.title: Your account gets deleted in 9 minutes
school-sch-01.prompt: A Discord message says your gaming account was reported for cheating and will be deleted in nine minutes unless you complete a “player appeal.” The link already shows your gamer tag and profile picture.
school-sch-01.answersA: Open the game’s official app/site yourself and check account notices or support there.
school-sch-01.answersB: Ask a parent, trusted adult, or friend to help verify the support message before logging in anywhere.
school-sch-01.answersC: Use the appeal link because it already knows your gamer tag and the timer is running.
school-sch-01.explanation: Public profile details are easy to copy. Real account actions should appear inside the game’s own support system.
school-sch-01.proTip: A countdown is trying to borrow your decision-making.

school-sch-02.title: The “exam leak” closes at midnight
school-sch-02.prompt: A class group chat suddenly shares a site claiming to have tomorrow’s exam questions. Access costs $8 and the page says the file disappears at midnight. Several classmates are debating whether to buy it.
school-sch-02.answersA: Ask a trusted classmate whether the school has warned about fake exam links before doing anything.
school-sch-02.answersB: Open the preview only, without paying, to see whether the questions look real.
school-sch-02.answersC: Do not pay or download it; tell a trusted teacher or school staff member that the link is circulating.
school-sch-02.explanation: Exam-leak bait can deliver malware, steal payment details, or create discipline problems even if the file is fake.
school-sch-02.proTip: If the “advantage” requires a risky link, the cost can be bigger than the exam.

school-sch-03.title: Two tickets. Five minutes.
school-sch-03.prompt: Someone in your school group chat offers two sold-out concert tickets at face value because their parents changed plans. They need payment in five minutes because “another buyer is waiting.”
school-sch-03.answersA: Send half now to hold the tickets, then the rest after they transfer them.
school-sch-03.answersB: Use a ticket platform with verified transfer and buyer protection, or skip the deal.
school-sch-03.answersC: Ask for a live screen recording showing the tickets inside the official ticket app before paying.
school-sch-03.explanation: Pressure makes a risky payment feel like the only way to keep the deal. Protection matters more than speed.
school-sch-03.proTip: A good deal should survive a safe payment method.

school-sch-04.title: Your password “expires today”
school-sch-04.prompt: An email with the school logo says your student password expires today and you will lose access to assignments unless you reset it before 6 p.m. The button opens a page that looks exactly like the school login.
school-sch-04.answersA: Close the email and open the school portal from your normal bookmark or school website to check for a reset notice.
school-sch-04.answersB: Ask school IT or a teacher through a known channel whether passwords are expiring today.
school-sch-04.answersC: Reset it through the email because losing assignment access would be worse than being cautious.
school-sch-04.explanation: Phishing pages often copy real school branding. The safest move is to start from the portal you already trust.
school-sch-04.proTip: Type or tap your own trusted route, not theirs.

school-sch-05.title: Copyright strike: 15 minutes to appeal
school-sch-05.prompt: Your creator account gets a DM saying a copyright complaint will remove your profile unless you appeal within 15 minutes. The account sending it has a platform-style name and logo.
school-sch-05.answersA: Take a screenshot and ask a trusted adult or experienced creator to help verify the message.
school-sch-05.answersB: Use the appeal link but stop if it asks for anything beyond your normal login.
school-sch-05.answersC: Check your account’s official notifications or help center directly instead of using the DM link.
school-sch-05.explanation: Fake moderation messages work because losing an account feels urgent. Real enforcement should be visible in the platform itself.
school-sch-05.proTip: Account panic is exactly when to leave the DM.

school-sch-06.title: The skin drop ends in 90 seconds
school-sch-06.prompt: A live stream says the first 500 viewers who connect their game account will get a rare skin. A timer is counting down and chat messages are full of people posting “got it!”
school-sch-06.answersA: Connect the account because the stream is live and other viewers say it worked.
school-sch-06.answersB: Check the game’s official news or store for the promotion before connecting your account.
school-sch-06.answersC: Ask a trusted friend to verify the promotion independently while you stay off the link.
school-sch-06.explanation: Live chat and countdowns can be faked or botted. Account-linking permissions can give away more than a skin is worth.
school-sch-06.proTip: Rare loot is not worth rare access to your account.

school-sch-07.title: Registration closes in one hour
school-sch-07.prompt: A message says your team was nominated for a regional competition, but registration closes in one hour. The form asks for your full name, date of birth, home address and a parent’s card for a “refundable entry hold.”
school-sch-07.answersA: Verify the competition through the school/coach or the organizer’s official website before entering personal or payment details.
school-sch-07.answersB: Ask a parent or coach to review the registration independently.
school-sch-07.answersC: Fill in the personal details now and wait on the payment field until someone confirms it.
school-sch-07.explanation: Urgency can turn an exciting opportunity into an identity-data grab. Verify the event before feeding the form.

school-sch-08.title: Delivery fee before lunch
school-sch-08.prompt: You are waiting for limited-edition sneakers when a text says the courier cannot deliver without a $2.18 address fee paid before noon. The message arrives on the expected delivery day.
school-sch-08.answersA: Ask a parent or trusted adult to help verify the carrier and tracking number.
school-sch-08.answersB: Pay the tiny fee because the timing matches the delivery perfectly.
school-sch-08.answersC: Check the order and carrier tracking in the retailer/carrier app or website you open yourself.
school-sch-08.explanation: Scammers rely on the huge number of people expecting packages. Small fees can collect card and personal data.
school-sch-08.proTip: Expected package, unexpected link: still verify.

school-sch-09.title: “Send the code before my dad sees”
school-sch-09.prompt: A friend messages from their usual account saying they accidentally sent a verification code to your phone and need it back immediately “before my dad sees I messed up.” A code arrives seconds later.
school-sch-09.answersA: Send the code because it arrived right after your friend explained the mistake.
school-sch-09.answersB: Do not send the code; contact your friend another way and check what account the code is actually for.
school-sch-09.answersC: Screenshot the message and ask a trusted adult or friend to help verify what is happening.
school-sch-09.explanation: Attackers often use a compromised friend account to trick you into giving away a code that resets your own account.
school-sch-09.proTip: Your security code is not someone else’s typo.

school-sch-10.title: The fundraiser link “closes tonight”
school-sch-10.prompt: A popular student posts that the club fundraiser is short of its goal and shares a new payment link that closes tonight. The cause is real, but the link is not the one the school used last week.
school-sch-10.answersA: Donate only through the school or club’s confirmed payment channel after checking the new link is approved.
school-sch-10.answersB: Ask the club adviser or treasurer through a known channel whether the payment link changed.
school-sch-10.answersC: Donate because the fundraiser itself is definitely real and the amount is small.
school-sch-10.explanation: Real causes can be used to redirect money. Verify the payment destination, not just the story.
school-sch-10.proTip: True cause, wrong link = wrong destination.

school-sch-11.title: A “Discord mod” needs verification
school-sch-11.prompt: A user with a moderator-style badge says your account was flagged for underage access and asks you to “verify ownership” by signing into a page they send. They say refusing may lock your server access.
school-sch-11.answersA: Ask a server owner or trusted moderator you already know whether the person is legitimate.
school-sch-11.answersB: Open the link if the badge looks official and the page uses the correct branding.
school-sch-11.answersC: Use Discord/game support through the official app or site and ignore verification links sent by another user.
school-sch-11.explanation: Badges and roles can be faked or copied. Account verification should happen in official settings, not a user-sent page.
school-sch-11.proTip: A badge is not a password-reset department.

school-sch-12.title: Your teacher “shared a private file”
school-sch-12.prompt: An email that looks like it came from a teacher says, “I added comments to your draft—open before class.” The link asks you to approve a new app to read your school files and email.
school-sch-12.answersA: Approve the app because the teacher really is reviewing your draft this week.
school-sch-12.answersB: Open the school drive/LMS yourself and look for the shared file there, or ask the teacher directly.
school-sch-12.answersC: Check the sender address carefully and ask a classmate whether they received the same message.
school-sch-12.explanation: A believable teacher context can hide an OAuth permission request that grants broad access without stealing your password.
school-sch-12.proTip: “Approve access” can be as powerful as “enter password.”

school-sch-13.title: IT wants your MFA approval
school-sch-13.prompt: A message in the school help chat says IT is testing login security and asks you to tap “Approve” on the sign-in notification that just appeared on your phone.
school-sch-13.answersA: Deny the prompt and contact school IT through the normal help desk or portal.
school-sch-13.answersB: Ask IT to open a ticket in the school system before you approve any login.
school-sch-13.answersC: Approve because the prompt arrived exactly when the IT message said it would.
school-sch-13.explanation: An MFA approval authorizes a login. Timing only proves the sender caused the prompt, not that the sender is IT.
school-sch-13.proTip: If someone asks you to approve their login, it is probably their login.

school-sch-14.title: The “game admin” can restore your item
school-sch-14.prompt: After an in-game item disappears, someone claiming to be an admin offers to restore it. They ask you to trade them another item first “to verify the inventory system is working.”
school-sch-14.answersA: Check the game’s official list of moderators/admin procedures before interacting further.
school-sch-14.answersB: Send a low-value item first because a real admin should be able to return it instantly.
school-sch-14.answersC: Use the game’s official support process and do not transfer items to someone claiming to be staff.
school-sch-14.explanation: Scammers use authority plus your frustration to make a “test trade” feel reasonable. Staff should not need your valuables to prove their tools.
school-sch-14.proTip: Real support does not need a sacrifice item.

school-sch-15.title: “Verification team” offers a blue badge
school-sch-15.prompt: A DM says your account is eligible for verification because your recent post is trending. The form asks for your login and a photo ID to “reserve your badge.”
school-sch-15.answersA: Complete the form because the platform already knows your account is trending.
school-sch-15.answersB: Check verification options inside the platform’s settings/help center and ignore the DM link.
school-sch-15.answersC: Ask a trusted adult or creator to review the message before sharing any ID.
school-sch-15.explanation: Fake verification offers target ambition and status. Identity documents and logins should not move through an unsolicited DM.
school-sch-15.proTip: A badge should never cost you control of the account.

school-sch-16.title: “Police cyber unit” messages you
school-sch-16.prompt: An account claiming to be local police says your username appeared in a cyberbullying complaint. They ask you to continue privately and send screenshots of your messages before they “decide whether to contact your parents.”
school-sch-16.answersA: Do not continue privately; tell a parent, guardian, teacher, or other trusted adult and verify any police contact through an official number.
school-sch-16.answersB: Save the message and account details without sending private chats back.
school-sch-16.answersC: Send a few screenshots to prove you did nothing wrong and avoid involving adults.
school-sch-16.explanation: Fear of authority can make private disclosure feel like the fastest escape. Legitimate concerns should be handled with trusted adults and verified channels.
school-sch-16.proTip: If authority asks a minor for secrecy, bring in a trusted adult.

school-sch-17.title: The tournament organizer needs your login
school-sch-17.prompt: An esports organizer emails saying your team passed qualifiers but your game account must be linked for anti-cheat checks. The link asks for your game username, password and an MFA code.
school-sch-17.answersA: Ask your coach/team lead to confirm the organizer and anti-cheat requirements.
school-sch-17.answersB: Link the account because anti-cheat systems legitimately need deep access.
school-sch-17.answersC: Verify the tournament on the official organizer/game site and use only its documented account-linking process.
school-sch-17.explanation: Real anti-cheat tools may need software or account permissions, but they should not ask you to hand over credentials through an email link.
school-sch-17.proTip: Legitimate deep access still comes through legitimate installation paths.

school-sch-18.title: You “won” a student award
school-sch-18.prompt: A polished email says you were selected for a youth scholarship and must upload a student ID plus pay a $15 processing fee to accept. It names your school and grade correctly.
school-sch-18.answersA: Pay the small fee because the email already knows your school details.
school-sch-18.answersB: Verify the scholarship through the organization’s official site and your school counselor before sending ID or money.
school-sch-18.answersC: Ask the organization to explain why a winner must pay a fee and provide formal terms.
school-sch-18.explanation: School details can be public or scraped. Legitimate awards should be independently verifiable before money or identity documents move.
school-sch-18.proTip: Winning should not start with paying.

school-sch-19.title: “Apple/Google Support” found a charge
school-sch-19.prompt: A pop-up says your app-store account bought $149 of game currency. A support chat opens automatically and asks you to install a profile so they can cancel the purchase.
school-sch-19.answersA: Close the pop-up and check purchase history in your actual app-store account; contact support from there if needed.
school-sch-19.answersB: Ask a parent or trusted adult to help review the account before installing anything.
school-sch-19.answersC: Install the profile but remove it after the refund is complete.
school-sch-19.explanation: Fake purchase alerts create urgency and borrow a trusted brand. Configuration profiles can grant powerful device access.
school-sch-19.proTip: Refunds do not require surrendering device control.

school-sch-20.title: Coach needs a new roster form
school-sch-20.prompt: A message that appears to come from your coach says the team is switching apps. The new roster form asks for your home address, date of birth, emergency contacts and a photo of a parent’s ID.
school-sch-20.answersA: Show the form to a parent/guardian and let them handle any sensitive identity fields.
school-sch-20.answersB: Fill in your own information now and leave the parent ID field for later.
school-sch-20.answersC: Ask the coach in person or through the team’s existing app whether the form is genuine before entering information.
school-sch-20.explanation: Teams legitimately collect information, which makes fake forms believable. Sensitive data should follow a verified school/team process.
school-sch-20.proTip: Real context does not automatically make a new form real.

school-sch-21.title: Your best friend needs one tiny favour
school-sch-21.prompt: Your best friend’s account asks you to help recover their social profile by sending them a code that just arrived on your phone. Their messages sound normal and reference a joke from last week.
school-sch-21.answersA: Send it because the private joke proves it is really your friend.
school-sch-21.answersB: Do not send the code; contact your friend another way and check what the code says it is for.
school-sch-21.answersC: Ask your friend to call or video you before doing anything with the code.
school-sch-21.explanation: Compromised accounts include old chats, photos and context. Private history can be read by whoever took the account.
school-sch-21.proTip: Inside jokes are not two-factor authentication.

school-sch-22.title: There is a video of you. Or is there?
school-sch-22.prompt: A classmate sends a link saying, “Someone made an AI video of you—this is bad.” The preview thumbnail looks like your face, but the site asks you to log in before viewing the full clip.
school-sch-22.answersA: Do not log in; ask the classmate what they saw and report the situation to a trusted adult/school if needed.
school-sch-22.answersB: Search your real social accounts or platform reports without using the link to see whether anything was posted.
school-sch-22.answersC: Log in quickly so you can see whether the video is real before more people watch it.
school-sch-22.explanation: Fear and curiosity are powerful click triggers. The safest first step is to protect your account and get help, not feed credentials to the link.
school-sch-22.proTip: You do not need to risk your account to investigate a rumor.

school-sch-23.title: Your online teammate wants to “borrow” your login
school-sch-23.prompt: A teammate you have played with for months says their account is temporarily banned and asks to use yours for one tournament match. They offer to send you a rare item afterward.
school-sch-23.answersA: Ask whether the tournament allows substitutes and help them find another solution.
school-sch-23.answersB: Share the account just for the match, then change the password immediately afterward.
school-sch-23.answersC: Do not share the account; suggest they use the game’s appeal process or sit out the match.
school-sch-23.explanation: Trust built through play is real, but shared credentials can lead to bans, theft or account recovery problems.
school-sch-23.proTip: Friendship does not make account sharing reversible.

school-sch-24.title: A private-image threat
school-sch-24.prompt: Someone you met online says they have a private or embarrassing image of you and threatens to send it to classmates unless you pay or send more images. They tell you not to tell anyone.
school-sch-24.answersA: Pay once to buy time and keep the image from spreading while you decide what to do.
school-sch-24.answersB: Do not pay or send more; save evidence and tell a parent, guardian, counselor, or other trusted adult immediately, and use the platform’s reporting tools.
school-sch-24.answersC: Block the account after saving evidence and ask a trusted adult to help with reporting and account security.
school-sch-24.explanation: Paying or sending more usually gives the person more leverage. Getting a trusted adult involved breaks the secrecy they depend on.
school-sch-24.proTip: Secrecy protects the scammer, not you.

school-sch-25.title: Vote for our class—one login
school-sch-25.prompt: A classmate posts a “best school spirit” voting link in the class chat and says everyone needs to vote twice. The page asks you to sign in with your school email to stop duplicate votes.
school-sch-25.answersA: Verify the contest through the school or organizer before using your school login.
school-sch-25.answersB: Ask the classmate where they got the link and check it with a teacher or school site.
school-sch-25.answersC: Sign in because school email is exactly how a contest would stop duplicate voting.
school-sch-25.explanation: A plausible reason for login does not make an unknown site safe. School credentials unlock far more than a vote.
school-sch-25.proTip: Your school account is worth more than a class poll.

school-sch-26.title: A creator wants you on the team
school-sch-26.prompt: A small creator you follow DMs saying they love your edits and want you in a paid “youth creator team.” They send a contract link that first asks you to connect your social account with full posting access.
school-sch-26.answersA: Ask for the contract as a PDF or document that does not require social-account access.
school-sch-26.answersB: Connect the account because the collaboration is about posting content anyway.
school-sch-26.answersC: Verify the creator through a public business contact and review any contract with a parent/guardian before granting account permissions.
school-sch-26.explanation: Account permissions can hand over posting, messages or recovery access. A real collaboration can be discussed before giving technical control.

school-sch-27.title: Your teammate needs gift cards
school-sch-27.prompt: A teammate messages that they forgot a parent’s birthday and cannot use their bank card. They ask you to buy a $30 gift card and send the code, promising to pay you tomorrow at practice.
school-sch-27.answersA: Buy it because the amount is small and you see the teammate every week.
school-sch-27.answersB: Verify with the teammate in person or by voice/video through a known number before buying anything.
school-sch-27.answersC: Offer to help them find another solution without sending a gift-card code.
school-sch-27.explanation: Compromised accounts often ask for small, believable favors. Gift-card codes are cash once shared.
school-sch-27.proTip: Small favor, irreversible payment: verify the person.

school-sch-28.title: Can I use your account for one day?
school-sch-28.prompt: A friend says they were unfairly banned from a social app and asks to use your account for one day to keep a streak and message their group. They promise not to change anything.
school-sch-28.answersA: Do not share the account; help them appeal or communicate through another safe channel.
school-sch-28.answersB: Offer to send one message on their behalf without giving them login access.
school-sch-28.answersC: Let them use it while you stay nearby and watch what they do.
school-sch-28.explanation: Even trusted friends can trigger bans, expose private messages or accidentally change recovery settings.
school-sch-28.proTip: If the account represents you, keep control of it.

school-sch-29.title: Mom’s voice says pickup changed
school-sch-29.prompt: During an after-school activity, you get a voice message that sounds like your parent saying a family friend will pick you up instead and asking you to leave through a different gate.
school-sch-29.answersA: Ask the supervising adult to verify the pickup change with your listed emergency contacts.
school-sch-29.answersB: Follow the voice message because you clearly recognize your parent’s voice.
school-sch-29.answersC: Confirm the change through the school/club’s normal pickup process or call your parent on the known number before leaving.
school-sch-29.explanation: Voice can be cloned or replayed. Physical-safety changes should always go through the trusted pickup process.
school-sch-29.proTip: For pickup changes, process beats voice.

school-sch-30.title: The shared notes need “extra access”
school-sch-30.prompt: A study-group member posts a link to a shared notes folder. When you open it, the site asks to connect to your school cloud account and approve access to email, files and contacts.
school-sch-30.answersA: Approve it because the study-group member is someone you know and the notes are real.
school-sch-30.answersB: Do not approve broad access; ask for the notes through the school’s normal drive or a simple file share.
school-sch-30.answersC: Check the app name and permissions with school IT or a trusted adult before connecting anything.
school-sch-30.explanation: The sender’s account may be compromised, and broad OAuth permissions can expose much more than the notes.
school-sch-30.proTip: A notes folder should not need your inbox.

school-sch-31.title: The poster promises free pizza
school-sch-31.prompt: A QR poster near school says, “Free pizza for students—claim your code.” The page asks you to sign in with your school account and then requests permission to read your profile and contacts.
school-sch-31.answersA: Do not sign in; verify the promotion through the school or restaurant’s official channel.
school-sch-31.answersB: Inspect the destination and ask school staff whether the poster is approved before entering anything.
school-sch-31.answersC: Sign in because the school account is only being used to prove you are a student.
school-sch-31.explanation: QR codes hide the destination until after you scan, and “student verification” is an easy excuse to collect credentials or permissions.
school-sch-31.proTip: Free pizza should not need access to your contacts.

school-sch-32.title: Send me the reset code
school-sch-32.prompt: Someone messages that they accidentally entered your phone number while recovering their account. A code arrives and they ask you to forward it so they can finish the reset.
school-sch-32.answersA: Block the requester and check recent login/recovery activity in your account.
school-sch-32.answersB: Send the code if the text does not show your username, because it might really be for them.
school-sch-32.answersC: Do not send it; read the message around the code and secure your own account if the code is for you.
school-sch-32.explanation: Recovery codes are often tied to your number or account even if the message is vague. Sharing them can hand over access.
school-sch-32.proTip: If a code lands on your phone, treat it as yours to protect.

school-sch-33.title: This filter wants your whole camera roll
school-sch-33.prompt: A trending AI photo app promises a “future self” image. Before it works, it asks for full photo-library access, contacts and precise location, even though you only want to upload one selfie.
school-sch-33.answersA: Allow everything once, create the image, then revoke permissions immediately.
school-sch-33.answersB: Deny unnecessary permissions and use an app that allows selecting only the photo needed.
school-sch-33.answersC: Check the app’s privacy information and ask a trusted adult before granting broad access.
school-sch-33.explanation: Data can be copied the moment permission is granted. Temporary access can still be enough to collect more than the feature needs.
school-sch-33.proTip: “I’ll revoke it later” is not the same as “they never got it.”

school-sch-34.title: The middleman has 10,000 followers
school-sch-34.prompt: You are trading a rare in-game item. The other player suggests a “trusted middleman” with a huge following who will hold both items. The middleman sends a trade link outside the game.
school-sch-34.answersA: Use the game/platform’s official trading system and avoid off-platform middlemen.
school-sch-34.answersB: Check whether the game recognizes any escrow or trade-protection system before proceeding.
school-sch-34.answersC: Use the middleman because the follower count and public reputation make a scam unlikely.
school-sch-34.explanation: Follower counts and reputation accounts can be bought or hijacked. The strongest protection is the platform’s own transaction control.
school-sch-34.proTip: Trade protection should come from the system, not a celebrity stranger.

school-sch-35.title: The “cheat” needs device admin
school-sch-35.prompt: A friend shares a cheat or mod that supposedly unlocks premium features. The installer asks you to disable security warnings and give it device-admin or accessibility permissions.
school-sch-35.answersA: Ask a trusted adult or technically knowledgeable person to explain what the requested permissions can do.
school-sch-35.answersB: Install it on a spare device first to see whether it works safely.
school-sch-35.answersC: Do not install it; remove the file and use only trusted app/game sources.
school-sch-35.explanation: Admin/accessibility permissions can let malicious apps read screens, intercept codes or control settings. A spare device can still expose accounts.
school-sch-35.proTip: A cheat that needs security disabled is telling you what it is.

school-sch-36.title: School-trip Wi-Fi wants your social login
school-sch-36.prompt: On a school trip, a café Wi-Fi page offers faster access if you log in with Instagram or TikTok. The page looks polished and the network name matches the café.
school-sch-36.answersA: Use the social login because it is faster and the café name matches the Wi-Fi network.
school-sch-36.answersB: Ask staff for the official network and use basic guest access without handing over a social-media password.
school-sch-36.answersC: Use mobile data or wait if the network requires an unrelated account login.
school-sch-36.explanation: Anyone nearby can create a network with the same name. Free Wi-Fi should not require credentials to an unrelated high-value account.
school-sch-36.proTip: The Wi-Fi needs internet access, not your social identity.

school-sch-37.title: “Support” wants to watch your phone
school-sch-37.prompt: Someone claiming to be game support says they can recover stolen items if you screen-share while opening your email and game account. They say you can stop sharing anytime.
school-sch-37.answersA: Do not screen-share sensitive accounts; use the game’s official support ticket system instead.
school-sch-37.answersB: Ask a trusted adult to help contact support through the official site.
school-sch-37.answersC: Share the screen but hide notifications and avoid typing your password on camera.
school-sch-37.explanation: Screen sharing can expose recovery links, codes and personal messages even without showing a password.
school-sch-37.proTip: Your screen can leak keys you never meant to say out loud.

school-sch-38.title: Your skin can become an “investment”
school-sch-38.prompt: A gaming community advertises a token tied to rare skins. The site says connecting your wallet will show the value of your inventory and offers a free token for first-time users.
school-sch-38.answersA: Use a wallet with no funds and no valuable assets if you are only researching how the site works.
school-sch-38.answersB: Connect your normal wallet but reject any transaction that asks to move money.
school-sch-38.answersC: Do not connect a wallet based on a community link; discuss any real-money investment with a parent/guardian and verify the project independently.
school-sch-38.explanation: Wallet connections and signatures can authorize more than a visible payment. “Free” tokens are common bait for risky permissions.
school-sch-38.proTip: A wallet signature can spend value without looking like a purchase.

school-sch-39.title: The invoice is in the DM
school-sch-39.prompt: A seller you follow sends an “invoice” in a DM for a limited hoodie drop. The button opens a payment page asking for your card plus your email password “to confirm the order account.”
school-sch-39.answersA: Pay if the card page looks secure, but leave the email-password field blank.
school-sch-39.answersB: Buy only through the seller’s verified storefront or platform checkout; never enter your email password into a shop payment page.
school-sch-39.answersC: Ask the seller to send the product link through their public profile/store instead of the DM.
school-sch-39.explanation: A shop should not need your email password. DM invoices bypass the protections of the normal storefront.
school-sch-39.proTip: Payment pages need payment data—not your inbox key.

school-sch-40.title: A “support bot” asks for your recovery words
school-sch-40.prompt: A support bot in a gaming marketplace says your wallet connection failed and asks you to enter the 12 recovery words so it can “resync ownership.”
school-sch-40.answersA: Never enter recovery words into support chat or a website; close it and use the wallet provider’s official recovery guidance.
school-sch-40.answersB: Ask a trusted adult or knowledgeable person to help verify the wallet issue without sharing the recovery phrase.
school-sch-40.answersC: Enter the words only if the page is inside the marketplace you already use.
school-sch-40.explanation: Recovery phrases are master keys to the wallet. No legitimate support process needs them to verify ownership.
school-sch-40.proTip: Recovery words are the wallet, not a support ticket.

school-sch-41.title: Free Discord Nitro - link expires tonight
school-sch-41.prompt: A DM from someone in your server says they're giving away free Discord Nitro, but the link only works for the next 20 minutes and needs you to log in.
school-sch-41.answersA: Log in quickly before the offer expires.
school-sch-41.answersB: Skip it. Real Nitro gifts come from Discord itself or a friend you already trust, not a countdown link in a DM.
school-sch-41.answersC: Log in, and also send the link to your friends before it expires.
school-sch-41.explanation: Fake Nitro gift links are one of the most common Discord phishing scams, built to steal your login the moment you enter it under a fake deadline.
school-sch-41.proTip: A countdown on a login page is designed to stop you from thinking - that's the whole trick.

school-sch-42.title: Your study app's free trial ends at midnight
school-sch-42.prompt: A pop-up in a homework-help app says your free trial ends at midnight and you'll lose your saved notes unless you enter a card number right now to keep using it.
school-sch-42.answersA: Check with a parent before entering any card details, and read what happens if the trial just ends.
school-sch-42.answersB: Enter your own details quickly so you don't lose your notes.
school-sch-42.answersC: Enter a parent's card number without asking, since it's just to save your notes.
school-sch-42.explanation: Free-trial pop-ups are designed to make losing your notes feel urgent, but a trial ending never deletes your existing account without warning - and a card decision isn't yours to make alone.
school-sch-42.proTip: A subscription decision always waits for a parent, no matter what the countdown says.

school-sch-43.title: A modelling scout saw your photos
school-sch-43.prompt: An account claiming to be from a modelling agency messages you, saying they've been watching your profile and want to sign you - but first you need to pay for a 'starter portfolio' and share more photos privately.
school-sch-43.answersA: Send a few more photos to see what they say.
school-sch-43.answersB: Don't pay or send anything privately; tell a parent or trusted adult about the message.
school-sch-43.answersC: Pay for the portfolio since real agencies find people this way.
school-sch-43.explanation: Real modelling and talent agencies don't recruit through DMs and don't ask a teenager to pay upfront or send private photos - that combination is a scouting scam.
school-sch-43.proTip: Being 'discovered' never comes with an invoice.

school-sch-44.title: School office: your lunch account is overdue
school-sch-44.prompt: A text that looks like it's from your school says your lunch account balance is overdue and asks you to pay through a link before your card is blocked at checkout.
school-sch-44.answersA: Pay through the link quickly so lunch isn't blocked.
school-sch-44.answersB: Forward the link to friends so they can pay too.
school-sch-44.answersC: Check the balance directly in the school's official payment app or ask the school office.
school-sch-44.explanation: School payment systems don't threaten to block your lunch by text with an outside link - a real balance issue shows up in the official app or a letter home.
school-sch-44.proTip: Go straight to the account you already have, not a link a text sends you.

school-sch-45.title: He only talks to you and says don't tell anyone
school-sch-45.prompt: An online friend you met through a game has become your main confidant. Lately he's started asking for photos and says it has to stay a secret between just the two of you, or he'll be hurt that you don't trust him.
school-sch-45.answersA: Send one photo to prove you trust him, then stop.
school-sch-45.answersB: Keep it secret since he asked, and see where it goes.
school-sch-45.answersC: Don't send anything, and tell a parent or trusted adult about the conversation, even though it feels private.
school-sch-45.explanation: Asking to keep a relationship secret from the people who protect you is a warning sign on its own, whatever else is happening in the conversation.
school-sch-45.proTip: Anyone who needs you to keep them secret from your family is asking for something they know is wrong.

school-sch-46.title: Everyone's doing the 'expose' poll
school-sch-46.prompt: A poll app going around your grade asks you to rank classmates and answer questions about them, and says it needs access to your contacts to 'unlock' more questions.
school-sch-46.answersA: Answer the questions but skip the contacts permission.
