school-sch-46.answersB: Don't use the app at all, and tell a friend why.
school-sch-46.answersC: Use it fully, including granting contacts access, since everyone else is.
school-sch-46.explanation: These apps exist to harvest contact lists and produce content that turns into bullying - the 'everyone's doing it' pressure is the mechanism, not a reason it's safe.
school-sch-46.proTip: An app that needs your contacts to work is collecting more than a poll answer.

school-sch-47.title: Complete human verification for 10,000 V-Bucks
school-sch-47.prompt: A video promises 10,000 free V-Bucks if you enter your username and complete a 'human verification' survey, which asks for your email password to confirm you're not a bot.
school-sch-47.answersA: Close it. Free item generators for paid in-game currency don't exist, and no verification step ever needs a password.
school-sch-47.answersB: Enter the username only, and skip the password part.
school-sch-47.answersC: Complete the whole survey, including the password, to get the reward.
school-sch-47.explanation: There is no legitimate way to generate paid in-game currency for free. The 'verification' step exists purely to collect your login and personal details.
school-sch-47.proTip: Anything free that needs your password is only free for the person collecting it.

school-sch-48.title: Get paid to post - just install our creator app
school-sch-48.prompt: A brand DM offers to pay you to post about their product, but first you need to install their 'creator app' from a link outside the app store to track your earnings.
school-sch-48.answersA: Install it, since it's just to track how much you're paid.
school-sch-48.answersB: Install it, and also share your login so they can 'verify' your account.
school-sch-48.answersC: Don't install anything outside the app store, and check whether the brand and offer are real before agreeing to anything.
school-sch-48.explanation: Real brand partnerships pay through normal platforms and never require installing an app from outside the official store just to be paid.
school-sch-48.proTip: A job offer that starts with installing an unknown app is the job.

school-school-red-flag-relay-SCH-W1.title: School Red-Flag Relay
school-school-red-flag-relay-SCH-W1.prompt: School online play: each player has 20 seconds to name one niche red flag from the last School card without repeating another player.
school-school-red-flag-relay-SCH-W1.answersA: Complete the relay with no repeats.
school-school-red-flag-relay-SCH-W1.explanation: School Red-Flag Relay: the purpose is to turn the last scenario into active recall, not passive reading. It rewards naming a precise safer action instead of giving vague advice.
school-school-red-flag-relay-SCH-W1.proTip: Use it only after a scenario card, never as a separate mini-game.

school-school-safer-channel-switch-SCH-W.title: School Safer-Channel Switch
school-school-safer-channel-switch-SCH-W.prompt: School online play: replace the risky channel in the last School card with the safest niche verification channel.
school-school-safer-channel-switch-SCH-W.explanation: School Safer-Channel Switch: the purpose is to turn the last scenario into active recall, not passive reading. It rewards naming a precise safer action instead of giving vague advice.
school-school-safer-channel-switch-SCH-W.proTip: Good answers name the exact channel: portal, app, saved number, official office, manager, IT, provider, or platform.

travelsafe-tra-01.title: Your bag has 12 minutes
travelsafe-tra-01.prompt: You are already through security when a text says the payment for your checked bag failed. It knows your flight number and warns the bag will be offloaded unless you pay €35 within 12 minutes.
travelsafe-tra-01.answersA: Show the message to airline staff or check the bag status in the airline app you open yourself.
travelsafe-tra-01.answersB: Search the airline website and call a support number you find there before paying.
travelsafe-tra-01.answersC: Use the text link but pay with a virtual card so your main card stays protected.
travelsafe-tra-01.explanation: A safer card does not make an unverified payment request safe. First confirm that the charge exists through a channel you control.
travelsafe-tra-01.proTip: Real urgency is a reason to verify faster, not skip verification.

travelsafe-tra-02.title: The last room, apparently
travelsafe-tra-02.prompt: A booking-site message says your hotel has a payment problem and your room will be released in 20 minutes unless you re-enter your card on an external page. The message appears inside the same thread as your real reservation.
travelsafe-tra-02.answersA: Call the hotel using a number from its official site and ask whether your reservation is at risk.
travelsafe-tra-02.answersB: Pay through the external page because the message appeared inside your genuine booking thread.
travelsafe-tra-02.answersC: Open the booking in the platform and contact the hotel or platform through its built-in support tools.
travelsafe-tra-02.explanation: Real booking accounts can be compromised, so the location of a message is not proof that its payment link is safe.
travelsafe-tra-02.proTip: A familiar thread can still contain an unfamiliar payment destination.

travelsafe-tra-03.title: Your visa needs “one final step”
travelsafe-tra-03.prompt: Two days before departure, a sponsored search result says your travel authorization is incomplete. The page knows the destination and offers “priority validation” if you pay a processing fee in the next hour.
travelsafe-tra-03.answersA: Pay the priority fee now, then verify the authorization later so you do not miss the trip.
travelsafe-tra-03.answersB: Close the ad and check your authorization on the official government site you type or navigate to yourself.
travelsafe-tra-03.answersC: Ask your airline whether your travel authorization appears valid in their check-in system.
travelsafe-tra-03.explanation: Travel-document anxiety makes paid “fast track” pages persuasive. Only the issuing authority can confirm the document status.
travelsafe-tra-03.proTip: For visas and entry permits, start with the government—not the ad.

travelsafe-tra-04.title: Tap to avoid a train fine
travelsafe-tra-04.prompt: A person wearing a rail-company vest says your mobile ticket did not validate. They point to a QR code on a handheld sign and say paying a €15 correction fee now avoids a much larger inspection fine.
travelsafe-tra-04.answersA: Ask to verify the issue at the staffed ticket desk or with the official rail app before scanning or paying.
travelsafe-tra-04.answersB: Ask the person to show official ID and explain exactly why your ticket is invalid.
travelsafe-tra-04.answersC: Scan the QR code and check whether the payment page shows the rail-company logo before paying.
travelsafe-tra-04.explanation: Uniforms and urgency can be copied. A genuine ticket problem should be verifiable in the operator’s own system.
travelsafe-tra-04.proTip: A uniform is a cue; the operator’s system is evidence.

travelsafe-tra-05.title: Sign here—the shuttle is waiting
travelsafe-tra-05.prompt: At rental-car return, an employee says a fresh wheel scratch will cost €480 unless you accept a €120 “rapid settlement” before the airport shuttle leaves. They want a signature on a tablet immediately.
travelsafe-tra-05.answersA: Ask a second employee or manager to inspect the damage before you sign anything.
travelsafe-tra-05.answersB: Accept the cheaper settlement so you do not miss your flight, then challenge it after you get home.
travelsafe-tra-05.answersC: Photograph the car, ask for the damage record and contract reference, and dispute or settle through the rental company’s official process.
travelsafe-tra-05.explanation: Time pressure at return is real, but signing can remove leverage. Preserve evidence and make the charge traceable through the company process.
travelsafe-tra-05.proTip: Your flight clock should not become someone else’s signature clock.

travelsafe-tra-06.title: Your connection just “moved”
travelsafe-tra-06.prompt: After a delay, a text says you have been auto-rebooked and must confirm the new flight within eight minutes. The route and original booking reference are correct, and the link opens a convincing airline login page.
travelsafe-tra-06.answersA: Log in through the link because the booking reference and route prove it is tied to your reservation.
travelsafe-tra-06.answersB: Open the airline app or airport departure board yourself and check the rebooking there.
travelsafe-tra-06.answersC: Go to an airline transfer desk or gate agent and ask them to confirm the new itinerary.
travelsafe-tra-06.explanation: Stolen itinerary data makes rebooking phishing unusually convincing. The safest move is to leave the incoming path entirely.
travelsafe-tra-06.proTip: Correct itinerary data proves knowledge, not identity.

travelsafe-tra-07.title: Airport eSIM: 70% off for six minutes
travelsafe-tra-07.prompt: A kiosk screen beside baggage claim advertises a “landing-only” eSIM deal with a six-minute countdown. The QR code installs a profile and asks you to sign in with your main email account to activate it.
travelsafe-tra-07.answersA: Buy or install an eSIM through a carrier or provider you independently choose, using its official app or site.
travelsafe-tra-07.answersB: Ask airport information whether the kiosk is an approved telecom seller before scanning anything.
travelsafe-tra-07.answersC: Scan it now but deny any permissions that look unrelated to mobile data.
travelsafe-tra-07.explanation: A countdown can make an unknown profile feel routine. You should know who controls the software or profile before installing it.
travelsafe-tra-07.proTip: Cheap data is not worth an unknown configuration profile.

travelsafe-tra-08.title: The ship sails. The link expires.
travelsafe-tra-08.prompt: While ashore, a WhatsApp message claiming to be your excursion operator says the return pickup point changed. It asks for a €25 “port access reissue” within ten minutes or your seat will be released.
travelsafe-tra-08.answersA: Ask another person in your booked group whether they received the same change and compare details.
travelsafe-tra-08.answersB: Pay the small fee so your seat stays protected, then ask for a refund onboard if it was unnecessary.
travelsafe-tra-08.answersC: Use the excursion voucher or cruise-line app to contact the operator through the number or channel you already had.
travelsafe-tra-08.explanation: Being far from the ship magnifies urgency. A real operator change should survive an independent callback through the original booking channel.
travelsafe-tra-08.proTip: When missing the ship is the fear, verify through the booking you already own.

travelsafe-tra-09.title: Your lounge pass “expires at boarding”
travelsafe-tra-09.prompt: A push notification says your lounge membership has a billing problem and will be suspended when boarding starts. You are standing outside the lounge and the notification offers a one-tap card update.
travelsafe-tra-09.answersA: Use the notification while you are physically at the lounge, because the timing makes the alert likely genuine.
travelsafe-tra-09.answersB: Open the lounge or card issuer app yourself and check membership status there.
travelsafe-tra-09.answersC: Ask the lounge desk whether your membership scans as active before changing any payment details.
travelsafe-tra-09.explanation: Physical context makes digital impersonation feel trustworthy, but the alert still controls the payment path.
travelsafe-tra-09.proTip: Being in the right place does not make an incoming link the right channel.

travelsafe-tra-10.title: Your suitcase is found—pay the courier
travelsafe-tra-10.prompt: Hours after reporting a missing bag, a message quotes your surname and baggage tag number. It says the suitcase is ready for delivery but a €18 courier fee must be paid within 30 minutes or delivery moves to tomorrow.
travelsafe-tra-10.answersA: Check the baggage-tracing portal or call the airline/baggage desk using the reference you received when you filed the report.
travelsafe-tra-10.answersB: Ask the sender for the airline case number, then compare it with your own report before doing anything else.
travelsafe-tra-10.answersC: Pay the small delivery fee because the baggage tag number would be difficult for a scammer to know.
travelsafe-tra-10.explanation: Baggage details can leak through tags, systems, or prior messages. Verify the delivery inside the claim channel you already established.
travelsafe-tra-10.proTip: Specific data can make a scam specific—not authentic.

travelsafe-tra-11.title: Your €486 refund is ready
travelsafe-tra-11.prompt: Your flight was cancelled yesterday. An email with the airline logo, your surname and the correct flight number says a €486 refund is ready, but the payment form expires in 30 minutes.
travelsafe-tra-11.answersA: Call the number in your original booking confirmation and ask whether a refund action is pending.
travelsafe-tra-11.answersB: Use the email link because the correct flight details show the airline already matched the message to you.
travelsafe-tra-11.answersC: Open the airline app or type its website yourself and check the cancelled booking and refund there.
travelsafe-tra-11.explanation: Correct booking details can be stolen or copied; they do not authenticate the sender. Verification should start outside the message.
travelsafe-tra-11.proTip: Correct details prove data access, not sender identity.

travelsafe-tra-12.title: “Border Police” wants a mobile fine
travelsafe-tra-12.prompt: You receive a call after crossing a border. The caller knows your nationality and says a camera recorded a customs violation. They text a payment link and warn that an unpaid fine could affect your return journey.
travelsafe-tra-12.answersA: Pay the fine by card if the text page uses the government crest and gives you a downloadable receipt.
travelsafe-tra-12.answersB: End the call and contact the border/customs authority through its official published channels to verify whether any case exists.
travelsafe-tra-12.answersC: Ask the caller for a case number and officer name, write them down, and verify them independently before taking action.
travelsafe-tra-12.explanation: Government branding and personal details are easy to imitate. The existence of a case must be verified independently.
travelsafe-tra-12.proTip: Authority should make verification stricter, not obedience faster.

travelsafe-tra-13.title: The front desk calls your room
travelsafe-tra-13.prompt: At 11:40 p.m., your room phone rings. “Front desk” says the hotel’s system lost your card authorization during a software update and asks you to read the card number again so they do not wake you later.
travelsafe-tra-13.answersA: Hang up and call the front desk using the button/number provided by the hotel, or walk down if practical.
travelsafe-tra-13.answersB: Ask the caller to state your reservation name and checkout date before deciding whether to continue.
travelsafe-tra-13.answersC: Give only the last four digits first; if they match the record, provide the rest.
travelsafe-tra-13.explanation: A call routed to your room can still be spoofed or socially engineered. Re-establish the conversation through a channel you initiate.
travelsafe-tra-13.proTip: If someone calls for secrets, hang up and call back on your terms.

travelsafe-tra-14.title: Security found your tablet
travelsafe-tra-14.prompt: A message says airport security recovered a tablet matching your lost-item report. It includes a photo that looks like yours and asks for a €9 identity-verification fee before the item can be released to the courier.
travelsafe-tra-14.answersA: Reply asking for the official case reference, then verify that reference on the airport site yourself.
travelsafe-tra-14.answersB: Pay the small fee because the attached photo proves they physically have the device.
travelsafe-tra-14.answersC: Use the airport’s official lost-property portal or phone number to check the case and release process.
travelsafe-tra-14.explanation: Photos and lost-item details can be copied from reports or social posts. The airport’s own case system is the reliable checkpoint.
travelsafe-tra-14.proTip: A photo proves an image exists; it does not prove who sent it.

travelsafe-tra-15.title: A “consular officer” has good news
travelsafe-tra-15.prompt: After you post online that your passport was stolen, someone messages from an account using your embassy’s seal. They say an emergency travel document can be issued today if you upload a selfie holding your passport copy and pay a courier fee.
travelsafe-tra-15.answersA: Send the selfie first but hold back payment until you receive a document number.
travelsafe-tra-15.answersB: Contact the embassy or consulate using contact details from the official government site and ask for the emergency-document procedure.
travelsafe-tra-15.answersC: Ask the account to email you from an official government domain, then compare the instructions with the embassy website.
travelsafe-tra-15.explanation: A public post gives impersonators both timing and context. Sensitive identity steps belong inside verified consular channels.
travelsafe-tra-15.proTip: Posting the problem publicly can invite private “official” help.

travelsafe-tra-16.title: The “police report” link
travelsafe-tra-16.prompt: A rental-company employee emails after your trip saying local police require an online statement for a traffic incident involving your car. The link asks for your licence, passport and card details before it shows the report.
travelsafe-tra-16.answersA: Open your rental account or contact the rental company through your contract details and ask whether any incident is attached to the rental.
travelsafe-tra-16.answersB: Ask for the police case number and agency, then verify the case with that agency independently.
travelsafe-tra-16.answersC: Complete only the identity fields first and stop if the site later asks for payment.
travelsafe-tra-16.explanation: A legitimate incident can still be used as bait. Verify the case before uploading a complete identity bundle.

travelsafe-tra-17.title: Claims says your bank “failed verification”
travelsafe-tra-17.prompt: A caller claiming to be from your travel insurer knows your claim amount and date. They say the payout failed and ask you to install a “secure verification” app so an agent can fix the bank details with you.
travelsafe-tra-17.answersA: Ask the caller to note the issue on your claim, then verify it later through your insurer account.
travelsafe-tra-17.answersB: Install the app but do not grant screen-control permission unless the insurer account shows the same request.
travelsafe-tra-17.answersC: End the call and open the insurer’s app/site or call the number on your policy to check the claim and payout details.
travelsafe-tra-17.explanation: Remote-access tools can turn a plausible service call into account theft. Payout changes should be verified in the insurer’s established channel.
travelsafe-tra-17.proTip: No claim is improved by giving a stranger control of your screen.

travelsafe-tra-18.title: The blue-check airline agent
travelsafe-tra-18.prompt: You post on social media that check-in is broken. Within two minutes, a verified-looking “Airline Help” account DMs you and asks for your booking code plus the one-time code it just sent “to open the reservation securely.”
travelsafe-tra-18.answersA: Send the one-time code because it arrived on your own phone, which confirms the airline has your number.
travelsafe-tra-18.answersB: Stop the DM and use the airline app, official site, or support handle linked from the airline’s own website.
travelsafe-tra-18.answersC: Give the booking code but refuse the one-time code until the account proves it is official.
travelsafe-tra-18.explanation: One-time codes often authorize account access; support should not need you to hand over a code that proves you are you.
travelsafe-tra-18.proTip: A code sent to you is usually for you—not for support.

travelsafe-tra-19.title: “Airport Free Wi-Fi” wants your email password
travelsafe-tra-19.prompt: A Wi-Fi network named after the airport opens a polished captive portal with airport branding. It offers free access if you “verify your identity” by signing in with Google or Microsoft.
travelsafe-tra-19.answersA: Ask airport staff for the official network name and connect only through the expected captive portal without handing over an unrelated account password.
travelsafe-tra-19.answersB: Use mobile data to check the airport website for Wi-Fi instructions before connecting.
travelsafe-tra-19.answersC: Use the Google/Microsoft sign-in because single sign-on is safer than creating a new airport password.
travelsafe-tra-19.explanation: A network name and logo are not authentication. Public Wi-Fi should not need credentials to an unrelated high-value account.
travelsafe-tra-19.proTip: Free Wi-Fi should not cost your email identity.

travelsafe-tra-20.title: The man with the airport badge
travelsafe-tra-20.prompt: At arrivals, someone with an airport lanyard says ride-hailing pickups have moved because of construction. He points to a printed QR code for the “temporary official taxi queue” and says app pickups are being cancelled.
travelsafe-tra-20.answersA: Ask the person where the official taxi rank is and walk there without scanning the code.
travelsafe-tra-20.answersB: Scan the QR code but compare the fare with your ride-hailing app before paying anything.
travelsafe-tra-20.answersC: Check the airport signs/app or ask the staffed transport desk where licensed pickups are actually operating.
travelsafe-tra-20.explanation: A badge and confident explanation can manufacture authority. Physical transport changes should be confirmed with the airport or operator.
travelsafe-tra-20.proTip: Confidence plus a lanyard is not a transport licence.

travelsafe-tra-21.title: Your travel agent needs your passport—again
travelsafe-tra-21.prompt: Your usual travel agent emails from the address you recognize and says the airline has changed its passenger-data rules. They attach a new portal link and ask you to upload passport scans for everyone on the booking by tonight.
travelsafe-tra-21.answersA: Use the link because the message came from the agent’s real address and they already know who is travelling.
travelsafe-tra-21.answersB: Call the agent on the number already saved in your contacts or open the agency portal yourself and verify whether new documents are actually required.
travelsafe-tra-21.answersC: Ask the agent to place the request inside the booking or established client portal before you upload anything.
travelsafe-tra-21.explanation: A familiar mailbox can be compromised, and passport scans are valuable enough to justify an independent check before uploading them to a new destination.
travelsafe-tra-21.proTip: Known sender, new document portal: verify the portal—not just the sender.

travelsafe-tra-22.title: Your sister is crying on the phone
travelsafe-tra-22.prompt: While you are abroad, a call from an unknown number sounds like your sister. She says her phone was stolen, she is in trouble, and she needs you to transfer money to a friend immediately before her battery dies.
travelsafe-tra-22.answersA: End the call and contact your sister through a known number, another family member, or a pre-agreed family verification question.
travelsafe-tra-22.answersB: Keep the caller talking while you message another family member from a second device to verify the story.
travelsafe-tra-22.answersC: Send a small amount first; if she confirms receipt, send the rest.
travelsafe-tra-22.explanation: Voice cloning and spoofed context can make emotional emergencies feel authentic. Independent family verification breaks the pressure loop.
travelsafe-tra-22.proTip: In a family emergency, verify the person—not the emotion.

travelsafe-tra-23.title: Your guide has a “new payment account”
travelsafe-tra-23.prompt: The guide from yesterday’s walking tour messages you by WhatsApp and offers a private day trip at a good price. The profile photo and chat history are familiar, but payment must go to a different name because “the company account is locked.”
travelsafe-tra-23.answersA: Ask the guide a detail from yesterday that was not posted publicly, then pay only through the original platform if available.
travelsafe-tra-23.answersB: Pay the new account because the existing chat history proves it is the same person.
travelsafe-tra-23.answersC: Contact the tour company or guide through the original booking platform and confirm both the offer and payment destination.
travelsafe-tra-23.explanation: A familiar account can be taken over. Payment destination changes are a high-value moment to re-verify identity.
travelsafe-tra-23.proTip: Old chat history does not guarantee the account still has its old owner.

travelsafe-tra-24.title: Forty percent bonus—everyone is sharing it
travelsafe-tra-24.prompt: A sponsored post uses your loyalty-program branding and promotes a 40% points-transfer bonus. Several travel accounts you follow have reposted it, but the destination domain is unfamiliar.
travelsafe-tra-24.answersA: Trust the offer if several established travel accounts shared it and the comments show successful transfers.
travelsafe-tra-24.answersB: Open your bank or loyalty app directly and look for the same transfer promotion there.
travelsafe-tra-24.answersC: Use support chat inside the official app and ask whether the promotion is active.
travelsafe-tra-24.explanation: Social proof can be bought, copied or amplified by compromised accounts. The offer should exist where your points already live.

travelsafe-tra-25.title: Your favourite creator has a secret rate
travelsafe-tra-25.prompt: A travel creator you follow posts a story offering followers a private hotel rate through a “partner portal.” The story looks normal, but the portal asks you to log in with your booking-site account before showing prices.
travelsafe-tra-25.answersA: Check the creator’s permanent profile/site and the hotel or booking platform independently before using any partner link.
travelsafe-tra-25.answersB: Message the creator through a previously known channel and ask whether the story is theirs.
travelsafe-tra-25.answersC: Use the portal if your password manager autofills the login, because that suggests the domain is legitimate.
travelsafe-tra-25.explanation: Creator accounts can be hijacked, and partner offers are perfect cover for credential phishing.
travelsafe-tra-25.proTip: A familiar face can front an unfamiliar domain.

travelsafe-tra-26.title: Your host needs “one more deposit”
travelsafe-tra-26.prompt: A week before check-in, your vacation-rental host says the building introduced a refundable security deposit. The message uses the same friendly tone as earlier chats and asks for payment by bank transfer to the owner’s spouse.
travelsafe-tra-26.answersA: Ask the host to add the deposit formally to the reservation so it appears inside the platform.
travelsafe-tra-26.answersB: Transfer it because the host has been helpful for weeks and the deposit is refundable.
travelsafe-tra-26.answersC: Check the platform rules and reservation terms, then confirm any new deposit through platform support before paying.
travelsafe-tra-26.explanation: Long, friendly communication builds trust, but new off-platform payments change the risk. Make the charge visible inside the booking system.
travelsafe-tra-26.proTip: Relationship history should not bypass payment controls.

travelsafe-tra-27.title: The group treasurer wants a quick top-up
travelsafe-tra-27.prompt: On a group trip, the person who has been collecting shared expenses messages that the restaurant deposit came out higher than expected. They ask everyone to send €80 to a new payment handle before dinner.
travelsafe-tra-27.answersA: Pay now because the amount is plausible and everyone else will probably do the same.
travelsafe-tra-27.answersB: Confirm the request with the person face-to-face or through a known number and verify the new payment handle before sending.
travelsafe-tra-27.answersC: Ask the group chat whether others saw the same request and whether the treasurer announced the new handle.
travelsafe-tra-27.explanation: Group context and plausible amounts lower suspicion. A changed payment destination still deserves direct confirmation.
travelsafe-tra-27.proTip: Familiar group, new payment handle: verify the handle.

travelsafe-tra-28.title: A forum veteran offers the missing miles
travelsafe-tra-28.prompt: A long-time member of a frequent-flyer forum offers to sell you the 12,000 miles you need for an award ticket. Their account is years old with many helpful posts, but they want payment by a method with no buyer protection.
travelsafe-tra-28.answersA: Use only the loyalty program’s permitted purchase/transfer route or a payment method with meaningful buyer protection.
travelsafe-tra-28.answersB: Check whether the forum account has recent activity and ask for references from prior transactions before deciding.
travelsafe-tra-28.answersC: Proceed because the old account and reputation make a takeover unlikely.
travelsafe-tra-28.explanation: Reputation accounts can be stolen, and off-platform point sales may also violate program rules. Old trust does not remove transaction risk.
travelsafe-tra-28.proTip: A respected account can still be a rented identity.

travelsafe-tra-29.title: Your holiday match has an “easy investment”
travelsafe-tra-29.prompt: Someone you met on a dating app during your trip has been chatting with you daily. After a few weeks they show screenshots of profitable trades and offer to guide you through a small crypto investment “just for fun.”
travelsafe-tra-29.answersA: Research the investment platform independently and ask a financially knowledgeable person you trust before doing anything.
travelsafe-tra-29.answersB: Try a very small amount first and withdraw it successfully before considering more.
travelsafe-tra-29.answersC: Keep romance and investing separate; do not fund or connect a wallet based on guidance from a new online relationship.
travelsafe-tra-29.explanation: Romance-investment scams often build trust over time and may allow small withdrawals to deepen commitment.
travelsafe-tra-29.proTip: A successful small withdrawal can be part of the script.

travelsafe-tra-30.title: Your pet sitter needs the alarm code
travelsafe-tra-30.prompt: Your pet sitter messages during your trip saying the smart lock stopped working and the alarm company needs the “master recovery code” shown in your security app. The sitter knows your pet’s routine and sends a photo from your front door.
travelsafe-tra-30.answersA: Send the master code because the photo proves the sitter is actually at your home.
travelsafe-tra-30.answersB: Contact the alarm/smart-lock provider through its official app or number and solve access without sharing a master recovery code.
travelsafe-tra-30.answersC: Call the sitter on the known number and verify the problem, then issue a temporary guest code if your system supports one.
travelsafe-tra-30.explanation: A real access problem does not make a master credential safe to share. Use temporary or provider-controlled recovery instead.
travelsafe-tra-30.proTip: Solve access with the least powerful credential possible.

travelsafe-tra-31.title: The taxi terminal is “down”
travelsafe-tra-31.prompt: At an airport taxi rank, the driver says the card terminal is offline and points to a QR code taped to the dashboard for cashless payment. The fare on the meter looks normal.
travelsafe-tra-31.answersA: Use the taxi company’s official payment method, ask for another licensed taxi, or pay through a verified terminal—not the loose QR code.
travelsafe-tra-31.answersB: Ask the airport taxi marshal or dispatch desk whether that QR payment method is approved.
travelsafe-tra-31.answersC: Scan the QR and pay a small amount first to see whether the driver confirms receipt.
travelsafe-tra-31.explanation: A correct fare does not authenticate a payment destination. Loose QR codes can redirect money or collect card details.
travelsafe-tra-31.proTip: Verify the destination before you verify the amount.

travelsafe-tra-32.title: The SIM kiosk wants two photos
travelsafe-tra-32.prompt: An airport SIM seller says local law requires a passport photo for activation. After taking it, the clerk also asks to photograph both sides of your bank card “for the payment file.”
travelsafe-tra-32.answersA: Use an official carrier shop or app instead if the kiosk cannot explain its data-handling process.
travelsafe-tra-32.answersB: Allow both photos if the clerk covers the security code on the back of the card.
travelsafe-tra-32.answersC: Verify what ID is legally required and pay through a normal terminal; do not allow a photo of your payment card.
travelsafe-tra-32.explanation: Some countries legitimately require ID for SIM registration, but that does not justify copying unrelated payment credentials.
travelsafe-tra-32.proTip: A legitimate ID requirement does not make every extra data request legitimate.

travelsafe-tra-33.title: A helpful stranger knows the trick
travelsafe-tra-33.prompt: An ATM keeps rejecting your card. A person nearby says that machine often “locks foreign cards” and offers to help you reset the transaction by inserting the card again while they guide you through the menu.
travelsafe-tra-33.answersA: Let the person guide you verbally while you keep possession of the card and cover the keypad.
travelsafe-tra-33.answersB: Cancel, take your card if possible, move to an ATM inside a bank or secure location, and contact your bank if the card is retained.
travelsafe-tra-33.answersC: Ask bank or venue staff for help without letting anyone touch the card or watch your PIN.
travelsafe-tra-33.explanation: Card-trapping and shoulder-surfing scams often rely on helpful strangers. Move the transaction to a controlled setting.
travelsafe-tra-33.proTip: When an ATM behaves strangely, change the machine—not your trust level.

travelsafe-tra-34.title: The terminal offers a “guaranteed rate”
travelsafe-tra-34.prompt: A shop terminal abroad asks whether to pay in your home currency or local currency. The cashier says the home-currency option is “guaranteed” and points to a rate on the screen that looks reassuring.
travelsafe-tra-34.answersA: Compare the offered conversion and usually choose local currency so your card issuer handles conversion under its terms.
travelsafe-tra-34.answersB: Ask the cashier to cancel and show the amount again in local currency before approving anything.
travelsafe-tra-34.answersC: Choose home currency because seeing the final amount removes exchange-rate uncertainty.
travelsafe-tra-34.explanation: Dynamic currency conversion can add a poor exchange rate or markup. The important action is understanding who sets the conversion.
travelsafe-tra-34.proTip: Choose the currency with eyes open, not because the terminal calls it convenient.

travelsafe-tra-35.title: The charger needs an app—via QR
travelsafe-tra-35.prompt: At a station, the only visible EV/phone charging instructions are a QR sticker saying “new app required.” The page opens an app-store-looking screen and asks for card details before download.
travelsafe-tra-35.answersA: Use another charger if you cannot confirm the operator and official payment method.
travelsafe-tra-35.answersB: Continue if the page shows the right charger number and location, because that data would be hard to fake.
travelsafe-tra-35.answersC: Find the operator name on the charger and get its app from the official app store listing or operator website you locate independently.
travelsafe-tra-35.explanation: Attackers can place QR stickers on real infrastructure and copy location details. The physical object is real; the QR destination may not be.
travelsafe-tra-35.proTip: Real machine, fake sticker is a powerful combination.

travelsafe-tra-36.title: You get an MFA prompt at the gate
travelsafe-tra-36.prompt: Right after an airline-support chat, your phone receives a login approval prompt for your airline account. The support agent says, “That’s me—tap Approve so I can fix your booking.”
travelsafe-tra-36.answersA: Approve once because the timing matches the support conversation, then change your password after the booking is fixed.
travelsafe-tra-36.answersB: Deny the prompt, end the chat, and reopen support through the airline app or site you navigate to yourself.
travelsafe-tra-36.answersC: Ask the agent to stop the login attempt and explain why account access is necessary before continuing.
travelsafe-tra-36.explanation: MFA approval authorizes a login; a support conversation does not make an unexpected login safe.
travelsafe-tra-36.proTip: MFA is a doorbell. Do not buzz in someone because they claim to be maintenance.

travelsafe-tra-37.title: Add this boarding pass to your wallet
travelsafe-tra-37.prompt: An email says your mobile boarding pass has been “reissued” after a seat change. The attachment asks you to install a wallet profile and sign in again to retrieve the new QR code.
travelsafe-tra-37.answersA: Open the airline app or official site and regenerate the boarding pass from your booking.
travelsafe-tra-37.answersB: Check the seat change with the airline before installing any profile or signing in through the attachment.
travelsafe-tra-37.answersC: Install the wallet item but stop if it asks for permissions beyond notifications.
travelsafe-tra-37.explanation: Boarding passes are easy to regenerate through the airline. There is no reason to trust an unsolicited profile or login flow.
travelsafe-tra-37.proTip: If an app can generate it, let the app generate it.

travelsafe-tra-38.title: Your forgotten jacket is “held by customs”
travelsafe-tra-38.prompt: A hotel says it mailed your forgotten jacket home. Two days later, a text claims customs is holding the parcel and asks for a small duty plus your passport number to release it.
travelsafe-tra-38.answersA: Contact the carrier using its official contact details and ask what information customs legitimately needs.
travelsafe-tra-38.answersB: Pay the small duty first because you are genuinely expecting a parcel, then provide ID only if the tracking updates.
travelsafe-tra-38.answersC: Use the tracking number from the hotel and the carrier’s official site/app to check whether customs action is actually required.
travelsafe-tra-38.explanation: Expected parcels make delivery scams especially convincing. The tracking route you already have is the safest source of truth.

travelsafe-tra-39.title: The merchant asks you to “verify” Apple Pay
travelsafe-tra-39.prompt: A merchant terminal declines your phone payment twice. The clerk says foreign wallets sometimes need manual verification and asks you to open your wallet settings while they scan a QR code shown on their terminal.
travelsafe-tra-39.answersA: Scan the QR but cancel if it asks for a password, recovery key or device-management permission.
travelsafe-tra-39.answersB: Stop and use another verified payment method or merchant terminal without changing wallet security settings from a QR prompt.
travelsafe-tra-39.answersC: Ask for a standard chip-and-PIN/card transaction and keep control of your device.
travelsafe-tra-39.explanation: Payment failure can be used to push you into an unrelated security flow. A merchant should not need access to wallet recovery or device settings.
travelsafe-tra-39.proTip: A declined payment is not a request to reconfigure your identity.

travelsafe-tra-40.title: The “official” map pin sells tickets
travelsafe-tra-40.prompt: You search Maps for a popular attraction and tap a listing that looks official. The booking page shows today nearly sold out and asks for your passport number plus full card details to issue “named-entry tickets.”
travelsafe-tra-40.answersA: Navigate to the attraction’s official website from a trusted source and compare ticket requirements and availability there.
travelsafe-tra-40.answersB: Call the attraction or tourist office through contact details you verify independently before entering identity data.
travelsafe-tra-40.answersC: Book through the map listing if reviews are numerous and recent, since fake listings rarely build that history.
travelsafe-tra-40.explanation: Search and map listings can be manipulated. High review counts do not justify unnecessary identity collection.
travelsafe-tra-40.proTip: A map pin is a discovery tool, not proof of ownership.

travelsafe-tra-41.title: Your booking is on hold - confirm in 30 minutes
travelsafe-tra-41.prompt: An email from a booking site says your hotel reservation is on hold and will be released in 30 minutes unless you re-enter your card details through the link provided.
travelsafe-tra-41.answersA: Log into the booking site directly through its app or a typed web address to check the reservation.
travelsafe-tra-41.answersB: Re-enter your card through the link to keep the booking.
travelsafe-tra-41.answersC: Re-enter your card, and also confirm the CVV by reply email.
travelsafe-tra-41.explanation: A real booking hold doesn't require re-entering full card details through an emailed link with a short countdown - that combination is a phishing pattern, not a booking system.
travelsafe-tra-41.proTip: Check a booking inside the app you booked with, not through a link that found you.

travelsafe-tra-42.title: Airport strike - rebook in the next 10 minutes
travelsafe-tra-42.prompt: During a real airport strike, a text with an airline logo says your flight is affected and you have 10 minutes to rebook through a link before all alternate seats are gone.
travelsafe-tra-42.answersA: Click the link and rebook quickly before seats run out.
travelsafe-tra-42.answersB: Click the link, and pay extra to guarantee priority rebooking.
travelsafe-tra-42.answersC: Go directly to the airline's official app or website to check your flight status and rebook there.
travelsafe-tra-42.explanation: Real disruptions are exploited by scam texts that copy the logo and urgency of a genuine airline alert - the actual rebooking always happens on the airline's own channel.
travelsafe-tra-42.proTip: A real disruption is confirmed on the airline's own app, not a text with a countdown.

travelsafe-tra-43.title: Official portal: pay your entry authorisation fee
travelsafe-tra-43.prompt: A search result leads you to a professional-looking site offering to process your travel entry authorisation for a service fee well above the government's own price, before your trip.
travelsafe-tra-43.answersA: Go to the government's own official domain directly to apply at the correct price.
travelsafe-tra-43.answersB: Pay through the site since it looks official and saves time.
travelsafe-tra-43.answersC: Pay through the site, and also upload a passport photo for 'fast processing'.
travelsafe-tra-43.explanation: Unofficial sites that rank highly in search results routinely charge a large markup for a form you can file yourself, directly on the government's real domain, for less.
travelsafe-tra-43.proTip: Type the government domain in yourself rather than trusting a search-ad result.

travelsafe-tra-44.title: Tourist police - settle this fine, card only
travelsafe-tra-44.prompt: Someone in uniform stops you on the street, claims you've broken a minor local rule, and says the fine must be paid immediately by card on a handheld device, or your passport will be held.
travelsafe-tra-44.answersA: Pay by card immediately to avoid losing your passport.
travelsafe-tra-44.answersB: Ask to see identification and a written citation, and offer to settle it at a police station instead.
travelsafe-tra-44.answersC: Hand over your passport and card together to resolve it faster.
travelsafe-tra-44.explanation: Genuine on-the-spot fines are rare and are documented with a written citation; a demand for immediate card payment with a passport threat is a well-known tourist shakedown.
travelsafe-tra-44.proTip: A real fine survives being paid at a station, with a receipt - a fake one doesn't.

travelsafe-tra-45.title: A local you met offers to change money
travelsafe-tra-45.prompt: Someone friendly you met at your accommodation offers to exchange your currency at a much better rate than any exchange office nearby, right there on the street.
travelsafe-tra-45.answersA: Exchange a small amount first to test it.
travelsafe-tra-45.answersB: Exchange your full remaining cash since the rate is so much better.
travelsafe-tra-45.answersC: Politely decline and use a licensed exchange office or your bank card instead.
travelsafe-tra-45.explanation: Street exchange offers that beat every licensed office are typically funded by counterfeit notes or short-counting, and the friendliness is part of lowering your guard.
travelsafe-tra-45.proTip: A rate too good for a licensed office to match usually isn't real money changing hands.

travelsafe-tra-46.title: Your host recommends their cousin's driver
travelsafe-tra-46.prompt: Your accommodation host warmly recommends their cousin as a private driver for the day, cash only, no app, saying it's cheaper and more reliable than booking one yourself.
travelsafe-tra-46.answersA: Book it since your host clearly trusts them.
travelsafe-tra-46.answersB: Book transport through a licensed app or your accommodation's official service instead.
travelsafe-tra-46.answersC: Book it, and pay the full day's fee upfront in cash.
travelsafe-tra-46.explanation: A warm personal recommendation removes the pricing transparency, receipts, and accountability that an app-based or licensed service provides, even when the host means well.
travelsafe-tra-46.proTip: Trusting your host doesn't require trusting an unlicensed driver with no receipt.

travelsafe-tra-47.title: The property messaged you - re-enter your card
travelsafe-tra-47.prompt: Through the booking platform's own messaging system, 'the property' says there was a payment issue and asks you to re-enter your card details on a linked page to keep your reservation.
travelsafe-tra-47.answersA: Re-enter your card through the link since the message came through the platform.
travelsafe-tra-47.answersB: Re-enter your card, and also send a photo of it for verification.
travelsafe-tra-47.answersC: Contact the platform's official support directly instead of using the link in the message.
travelsafe-tra-47.explanation: Compromised host accounts are used to message guests through the real platform, making the request look legitimate - the platform itself never asks for card details through a chat link.
travelsafe-tra-47.proTip: A message coming through the real app doesn't guarantee the request inside it is real.

travelsafe-tra-48.title: Your stolen phone: tap to see its location
travelsafe-tra-48.prompt: Hours after your phone was stolen, you get an email on another device: 'tap here to see your phone's current location,' asking you to log in to confirm it's really you.
travelsafe-tra-48.answersA: Log in through the link to try to track the phone quickly.
travelsafe-tra-48.answersB: Go directly to the official Find My / device-manager app or website instead of the emailed link.
travelsafe-tra-48.answersC: Log in through the link, and also share the passcode when it asks.
travelsafe-tra-48.explanation: After a theft, scammers send lookalike 'find your device' emails to phish the very account credentials that would let them unlock and resell the stolen phone.
travelsafe-tra-48.proTip: Track a stolen device through the real app you already have, not a link that emailed you first.

travelsafe-travelsafe-red-flag-relay-TRA.title: TravelSafe Red-Flag Relay
