workplace-wrk-01.title: New bank details before close
workplace-wrk-01.prompt: A long-standing supplier emails at 4:42 p.m. saying today’s €84,000 invoice must be paid to a new account because its bank is “under maintenance.” The thread contains real prior correspondence and the quarter closes today.
workplace-wrk-01.answersA: Pause the payment and verify the bank change through a known supplier contact and your normal change-control process.
workplace-wrk-01.answersB: Ask the supplier to confirm the change through your procurement portal or another established channel.
workplace-wrk-01.answersC: Send a small test payment so the main invoice can still be released before close.
workplace-wrk-01.explanation: Compromised threads make payment-diversion fraud look routine. A test transfer proves only that the destination can receive money.
workplace-wrk-01.proTip: New bank details are a verification event, not an accounting update.

workplace-wrk-02.title: Payroll closes in 20 minutes
workplace-wrk-02.prompt: An employee emails HR saying they changed banks and need their salary redirected before payroll closes. The message has the employee’s normal signature and mentions their upcoming vacation.
workplace-wrk-02.answersA: Hold the payroll change and ask the employee to update details through the HR system after identity verification.
workplace-wrk-02.answersB: Change it now because delaying salary would harm the employee and the email context is convincing.
workplace-wrk-02.answersC: Use the organization’s verified payroll-change process and confirm the employee through a known channel before changing bank details.
workplace-wrk-02.explanation: Attackers use urgency and personal context to redirect salary. Payroll destinations should change only through a controlled identity process.
workplace-wrk-02.proTip: Payday pressure should strengthen payroll controls, not bypass them.

workplace-wrk-03.title: The CEO needs gift cards between flights
workplace-wrk-03.prompt: A message from the CEO’s display name says they are boarding a flight and need 20 gift cards for client thank-yous within 30 minutes. They ask you to send the codes by text and promise to explain later.
workplace-wrk-03.answersA: Buy the cards now but keep the codes until the CEO lands and confirms.
workplace-wrk-03.answersB: Verify the request through a known executive assistant/CEO channel and follow procurement policy before purchasing anything.
workplace-wrk-03.answersC: Ask for the request to be placed through the normal purchasing workflow, even if that means missing the deadline.
workplace-wrk-03.explanation: Executive urgency and secrecy are classic social-engineering levers. Holding the codes still creates unnecessary exposure and sunk-cost pressure.
workplace-wrk-03.proTip: Urgent executive requests still belong inside normal controls.

workplace-wrk-04.title: Vendor says shipment leaves in an hour
workplace-wrk-04.prompt: A supplier says a production-critical shipment will miss pickup unless a wire is released within an hour. They attach a revised invoice with new beneficiary details and copy several familiar contacts.
workplace-wrk-04.answersA: Verify the beneficiary change through a known supplier contact and internal approval process before releasing the wire.
workplace-wrk-04.answersB: Escalate the business urgency internally while holding the payment until verification is complete.
workplace-wrk-04.answersC: Send part of the wire to secure the shipment while procurement verifies the rest.
workplace-wrk-04.explanation: Operational urgency can make a payment change feel unavoidable. Partial payments are still losses if the destination is fraudulent.
workplace-wrk-04.proTip: Protect the payment path first; solve the shipping urgency second.

workplace-wrk-05.title: DocuSign expires at 5 p.m.
workplace-wrk-05.prompt: You receive an e-signature notice for a contract you expected, and the email says the envelope expires at 5 p.m. The link opens a login screen asking for your Microsoft credentials before showing the document.
workplace-wrk-05.answersA: Contact the sender through the existing business thread or contract system to confirm the envelope.
workplace-wrk-05.answersB: Use the email link because you were expecting the contract and the deadline is real.
workplace-wrk-05.answersC: Open the e-signature service or contract system independently and locate the expected document there.
workplace-wrk-05.explanation: Expected documents make credential phishing more effective. The contract can be verified through the platform or sender without trusting the email link.
workplace-wrk-05.proTip: Expected content does not authenticate the delivery path.

workplace-wrk-06.title: “Reset now” during an outage
workplace-wrk-06.prompt: During a real company outage, a message in a large chat channel says IT is forcing password resets and links to an emergency portal. Colleagues are posting that they cannot access systems.
workplace-wrk-06.answersA: Use the emergency link because the outage itself proves an IT incident is happening.
workplace-wrk-06.answersB: Use the official IT status/help channel or identity portal you already know, not a link dropped into chat during the incident.
workplace-wrk-06.answersC: Contact the help desk through a known route and ask whether password resets are part of the incident response.
workplace-wrk-06.explanation: Attackers exploit real incidents because users expect unusual instructions. The event may be real while the recovery link is fake.
workplace-wrk-06.proTip: Real outage, fake fix is still a breach.

workplace-wrk-07.title: Quarter-end discount expires tonight
workplace-wrk-07.prompt: A reseller offers a steep quarter-end discount if you sign a revised order form and pay a deposit today. The rep has worked with your company before, but the payment link goes to a new portal.
workplace-wrk-07.answersA: Verify the portal and payment instructions through the vendor account team and your procurement process before committing funds.
workplace-wrk-07.answersB: Ask for the quote/order to be issued through the vendor’s established customer portal.
workplace-wrk-07.answersC: Pay the deposit because the rep and discount are both plausible and procurement can reconcile later.
workplace-wrk-07.explanation: Legitimate sales pressure can be copied by attackers or abused after account compromise. New payment infrastructure deserves independent verification.
workplace-wrk-07.proTip: A real discount does not make a new portal trustworthy.

workplace-wrk-08.title: Refund this customer before they escalate
workplace-wrk-08.prompt: A senior support agent messages finance saying a VIP customer was double-charged and needs an immediate refund to a different card/account because the original card was closed. The customer is threatening to post publicly.
workplace-wrk-08.answersA: Escalate the customer experience issue while keeping the refund tied to approved payment controls.
workplace-wrk-08.answersB: Send the refund to the new destination to prevent reputational damage, then document the exception.
workplace-wrk-08.answersC: Follow the documented refund process and verify the customer/payment destination before sending funds elsewhere.
workplace-wrk-08.explanation: Reputation pressure can be weaponized to bypass refund controls. Destination changes are exactly where verification matters.
workplace-wrk-08.proTip: Urgent customer care is not an exception to payment integrity.

workplace-wrk-09.title: Preserve these files in 30 minutes
workplace-wrk-09.prompt: An email labeled “Legal Hold – Immediate” says the company has 30 minutes to preserve evidence and asks you to upload project files to an external secure-transfer portal. The sender name matches outside counsel.
workplace-wrk-09.answersA: Upload because legal-hold deadlines can be strict and delaying could create liability.
workplace-wrk-09.answersB: Verify the legal hold with internal legal counsel or the known outside-counsel contact before uploading confidential files.
workplace-wrk-09.answersC: Preserve the files internally first while the transfer destination is verified.
workplace-wrk-09.explanation: Legal urgency can make unusual data movement seem necessary. Preserve first, transfer only after verifying destination and authority.
workplace-wrk-09.proTip: A deadline can justify preservation, not an unverified upload.

workplace-wrk-10.title: The executive is stranded—rebook now
workplace-wrk-10.prompt: An executive assistant account messages that the CEO is stranded after a cancellation and asks you to use a new travel portal to rebook immediately. The portal requests your corporate SSO login and card details.
workplace-wrk-10.answersA: Use the company’s approved travel provider or independently verified airline channels, and confirm the assistant request through a known route.
workplace-wrk-10.answersB: Call the travel desk or assistant on a known number and solve the itinerary through existing tools.
workplace-wrk-10.answersC: Use the portal because executive travel disruptions often require exceptions and speed.
workplace-wrk-10.explanation: Attackers exploit travel chaos and executive pressure to capture credentials and payment data. Existing travel channels are still safer.
workplace-wrk-10.proTip: An executive emergency is not an SSO exception.

workplace-wrk-11.title: The CEO is on the phone. Sort of.
workplace-wrk-11.prompt: You receive a call that sounds exactly like the CEO, including familiar speech patterns. They say an acquisition is confidential and instruct you to send a large payment before the market opens.
workplace-wrk-11.answersA: Ask a second authorized executive to confirm the transaction before doing anything.
workplace-wrk-11.answersB: Proceed because the voice, confidential context and timing match a real acquisition rumor inside the company.
workplace-wrk-11.answersC: Pause and verify the request through established payment approvals and a separate known channel to the CEO/executive team.
workplace-wrk-11.explanation: Voice cloning can reproduce tone and cadence. High-value decisions need process-based authentication, not voice familiarity.
workplace-wrk-11.proTip: A convincing voice is not a second approver.

workplace-wrk-12.title: IT wants remote control
workplace-wrk-12.prompt: A caller ID shows the company help desk. The caller says your laptop is beaconing to a malicious server and asks you to install a remote-support tool and sign in so they can “clean the token cache.”
workplace-wrk-12.answersA: Install the tool but watch the screen closely and stop the session if they open email or finance systems.
workplace-wrk-12.answersB: End the call and contact IT through the official help desk or ticket system before installing or granting remote access.
workplace-wrk-12.answersC: Disconnect from sensitive systems and create an IT ticket through the normal channel.
workplace-wrk-12.explanation: Remote-control access can expose tokens and credentials before anything obviously suspicious appears.
workplace-wrk-12.proTip: Verify support before support controls the device.

workplace-wrk-13.title: Your bank’s fraud desk calls finance
workplace-wrk-13.prompt: A caller claiming to be the company’s bank says a wire is being held for fraud review. They know the company name and recent transfer amount and ask for a security code to release the hold.
workplace-wrk-13.answersA: End the call and contact the bank using the treasury portal or known relationship-manager number.
workplace-wrk-13.answersB: Freeze or review the transfer in the bank portal while independently contacting the bank.
workplace-wrk-13.answersC: Read the code because the caller already knows the exact transfer amount.
workplace-wrk-13.explanation: Transaction details can leak through compromised email or systems. Security codes may authorize rather than cancel activity.
workplace-wrk-13.proTip: Knowing the transaction is not the same as controlling the bank.

workplace-wrk-14.title: Benefits team needs your login
workplace-wrk-14.prompt: A message from “HR Benefits” says open enrollment data did not migrate correctly and asks employees to reauthenticate through a portal using corporate SSO plus a personal tax/social-security number.
workplace-wrk-14.answersA: Check the official HR calendar/announcement channel to see whether a migration issue exists.
workplace-wrk-14.answersB: Use the portal because benefits enrollment legitimately involves personal identifiers.
workplace-wrk-14.answersC: Use the HR system from the company intranet or contact HR through a known channel before entering sensitive data.
workplace-wrk-14.explanation: Legitimate HR processes do involve sensitive data, making impersonation especially effective. Start from the HR system you already trust.
workplace-wrk-14.proTip: Sensitive context requires a stronger channel, not weaker skepticism.

workplace-wrk-15.title: Outside counsel requests a data dump
workplace-wrk-15.prompt: An email from a partner at outside counsel says regulators requested an urgent data set and asks you to upload customer records to a secure file-sharing link. The partner’s signature and matter number are correct.
workplace-wrk-15.answersA: Upload because the matter number and partner identity are correct and legal deadlines are sensitive.
workplace-wrk-15.answersB: Verify the request with internal legal and the known counsel contact before moving data outside approved systems.
workplace-wrk-15.answersC: Ask for the request to be placed in the established matter/document-sharing system.
workplace-wrk-15.explanation: Matter details can be available in compromised mailboxes. Data-transfer authority must be verified independently.
workplace-wrk-15.proTip: Correct matter, wrong destination is still exfiltration.

workplace-wrk-16.title: “Microsoft admin” needs a consent grant
workplace-wrk-16.prompt: A support engineer claiming to be from your cloud provider says a tenant issue requires temporary admin consent. They send a link that opens a genuine provider login page and asks you to approve a third-party application.
workplace-wrk-16.answersA: Do not grant consent from the incoming link; verify the support case in the provider portal and involve your internal admin/security team.
workplace-wrk-16.answersB: Ask the engineer to document the required permissions inside the official support ticket.
workplace-wrk-16.answersC: Approve because the login page is genuinely hosted by the cloud provider.
workplace-wrk-16.explanation: OAuth consent can grant broad access through a real provider page. The app and support case—not the login screen—must be verified.
workplace-wrk-16.proTip: Real login page, potentially malicious app.

workplace-wrk-17.title: A regulator wants records today
workplace-wrk-17.prompt: A caller says they are from a regulator conducting a spot audit and need employee/customer records by end of day. They provide names of your executives and cite a real regulation.
workplace-wrk-17.answersA: Ask for a formal written request and reference number, then verify it independently.
workplace-wrk-17.answersB: Send a limited sample first to show cooperation while legal checks the request.
workplace-wrk-17.answersC: Route the request to legal/compliance and verify the regulator through official agency contact information before sending data.
workplace-wrk-17.explanation: Regulatory language and public executive data are easy to borrow. Any disclosure still requires verified authority and scope.
workplace-wrk-17.proTip: Cooperation starts with verifying who you are cooperating with.

workplace-wrk-18.title: The supplier CEO wants an exception
workplace-wrk-18.prompt: A supplier CEO emails your procurement lead directly, apologizing for an internal banking issue and asking for a one-time payment exception to keep your order on schedule. The email domain looks nearly identical to the supplier’s.
workplace-wrk-18.answersA: Approve because a CEO-level request explains why the normal process is being bypassed.
workplace-wrk-18.answersB: Verify the request with known supplier contacts and your vendor-change process before any exception.
workplace-wrk-18.answersC: Escalate internally and ask the supplier to use its established commercial channel.
workplace-wrk-18.explanation: Authority can be used to justify the very exception that removes protection. Near-lookalike domains are a common impersonation tactic.
workplace-wrk-18.proTip: The higher the authority, the less reason to bypass controls silently.

workplace-wrk-19.title: A board member asks for the cap table
workplace-wrk-19.prompt: A board member’s personal email asks finance to send the latest cap table and option-grant details to a private address before a flight. The request sounds plausible and time-sensitive.
workplace-wrk-19.answersA: Verify the request and approved delivery channel through corporate governance/legal processes before sending sensitive data.
workplace-wrk-19.answersB: Ask the board member to retrieve the information through the board portal or approved document system.
workplace-wrk-19.answersC: Send a password-protected file to the personal email and share the password by text.
workplace-wrk-19.explanation: Encryption does not fix an unverified recipient or unauthorized channel. Governance data should stay inside approved systems.
workplace-wrk-19.proTip: Protect the identity and channel before protecting the attachment.

workplace-wrk-20.title: “Fraud prevention” wants a test payment
workplace-wrk-20.prompt: A bank security caller says your treasury account was targeted and asks you to make a $1 test transfer to a new beneficiary so they can confirm that transaction controls are working.
workplace-wrk-20.answersA: Lock/highly restrict outgoing payments while independently verifying the alert.
workplace-wrk-20.answersB: Send the $1 because the amount is negligible and can confirm whether the caller is truly watching the account.
workplace-wrk-20.answersC: Do not make the transfer; contact the bank through the treasury portal or known relationship manager.
workplace-wrk-20.explanation: A test payment only proves the destination received your money. It does not authenticate the caller and may establish a beneficiary for later fraud.

workplace-wrk-21.title: The email thread is real; the bank account is new
workplace-wrk-21.prompt: A supplier replies inside a months-old invoice thread and says future payments should go to a new bank account after a merger. The writing style and signatures match earlier messages.
workplace-wrk-21.answersA: Trust the change because the attacker would need access to the real thread to reply inside it.
workplace-wrk-21.answersB: Verify the bank change through a known supplier contact and approved vendor-master process outside the email thread.
workplace-wrk-21.answersC: Ask the supplier to confirm the change in your procurement/vendor portal.
workplace-wrk-21.explanation: Business email compromise often uses genuine compromised mailboxes and real threads. Thread continuity is not payment authentication.
workplace-wrk-21.proTip: A real thread can carry a fraudulent destination.

workplace-wrk-22.title: Your coworker sends a Teams file
workplace-wrk-22.prompt: A coworker messages you in Teams: “Can you review this before the meeting?” The link opens a login page and then asks to approve a new app with access to files, messages and contacts.
workplace-wrk-22.answersA: Ask the coworker through another channel or open the shared workspace directly; do not approve broad app access from the message.
workplace-wrk-22.answersB: Check the app publisher and permissions with IT/security before approving anything.
workplace-wrk-22.answersC: Approve because the message came from the coworker’s real Teams account.
workplace-wrk-22.explanation: Compromised collaboration accounts are powerful because they inherit trust. OAuth access can be malicious even through a real login page.

workplace-wrk-23.title: A familiar HR partner needs employee data
workplace-wrk-23.prompt: Your usual HR business partner messages asking for a spreadsheet of employee home addresses for an urgent benefits mailing. They use the same friendly tone and reference a real project.
workplace-wrk-23.answersA: Ask the HR partner to open the request in the standard HR/data process.
workplace-wrk-23.answersB: Send it because the requester is someone you work with every week and the project is real.
workplace-wrk-23.answersC: Verify the request and data-sharing need through an approved HR channel and send only via the authorized system if legitimate.
workplace-wrk-23.explanation: Compromised accounts and social engineering exploit real relationships. Sensitive employee data should follow process regardless of familiarity.
workplace-wrk-23.proTip: Familiar person, sensitive data: verify the request, not the tone.

workplace-wrk-24.title: A customer replies with a “diagnostic file”
workplace-wrk-24.prompt: A long-term enterprise customer replies in an existing support ticket with a ZIP file they say contains logs. They apologize for the size and ask you to run a small viewer included in the archive.
workplace-wrk-24.answersA: Run it because the customer is trusted and the file is inside a real support ticket.
workplace-wrk-24.answersB: Use approved malware-scanning/sandbox and support procedures; do not run customer-provided executables on your workstation.
workplace-wrk-24.answersC: Ask the customer to provide logs in a safe text/export format through the support portal.
workplace-wrk-24.explanation: Trusted customers can be compromised, and legitimate support context is useful cover for malware.
workplace-wrk-24.proTip: Trust the customer relationship; distrust executable attachments.

workplace-wrk-25.title: Your colleague has a new phone
workplace-wrk-25.prompt: A colleague messages from their normal account saying they replaced their phone and cannot access MFA. They ask you to approve a device-registration request because “IT said a teammate can vouch for me.”
workplace-wrk-25.answersA: Do not approve; direct them to the official identity-recovery/help-desk process.
workplace-wrk-25.answersB: Call the colleague on a known number and help them contact IT without approving any security request yourself.
workplace-wrk-25.answersC: Approve because you personally know the colleague and can confirm they really got a new phone.
workplace-wrk-25.explanation: Knowing the person does not authorize bypassing identity controls, and their account may be compromised.
workplace-wrk-25.proTip: Friendship is not an MFA recovery method.

workplace-wrk-26.title: The trusted consultant needs OAuth access
workplace-wrk-26.prompt: A consultant you have worked with for a year says their reporting tool was upgraded and asks you to reconnect your company account. The consent screen now requests broader permissions than before.
workplace-wrk-26.answersA: Ask for vendor documentation explaining the permission change and whether a least-privilege option exists.
workplace-wrk-26.answersB: Approve because the consultant and tool are already trusted vendors.
workplace-wrk-26.answersC: Pause and verify the new permission scope with the consultant and internal IT/security before reauthorizing.
workplace-wrk-26.explanation: Trusted vendors can change, be compromised, or request excessive permissions. Prior trust does not automatically extend to new access.
workplace-wrk-26.proTip: Old vendor, new permissions = new decision.

workplace-wrk-27.title: The partner moves the deal to WhatsApp
workplace-wrk-27.prompt: A partner you know emails that their corporate messaging is down and asks to continue a sensitive deal over WhatsApp. A new number then sends revised payment instructions.
workplace-wrk-27.answersA: Proceed because the initial email came from the partner’s real address and the outage could be genuine.
workplace-wrk-27.answersB: Verify the channel switch and payment instructions through a known corporate contact before acting.
workplace-wrk-27.answersC: Keep the deal paused until the partner’s normal systems or approved communication route are restored.
workplace-wrk-27.explanation: A compromised mailbox can redirect a conversation to an attacker-controlled channel, where later instructions look continuous.
workplace-wrk-27.proTip: Channel switching can be the attack, not a convenience.

workplace-wrk-28.title: The shared drive link is from the project lead
workplace-wrk-28.prompt: A project lead shares a “new secure folder” in chat for confidential launch materials. The link asks you to sign in and approve access to your entire cloud drive.
workplace-wrk-28.answersA: Open the company drive directly and locate the folder, or verify the link with the project lead through another channel.
workplace-wrk-28.answersB: Ask IT/security whether the new storage tool is approved before granting access.
workplace-wrk-28.answersC: Approve because the project lead is trusted and the launch really is confidential.
workplace-wrk-28.explanation: Confidentiality language can make broad access sound necessary. A simple folder should not need full-drive permissions.
workplace-wrk-28.proTip: More sensitive project means less tolerance for unknown tools.

workplace-wrk-29.title: The client says: “Use my Gmail today”
workplace-wrk-29.prompt: A long-standing client emails from their normal corporate account saying their document system is down. They ask you to send a confidential customer file to a personal Gmail address “just for today” so a deadline is not missed.
workplace-wrk-29.answersA: Hold the file until the client can provide an approved alternative channel or your security/privacy team authorizes one.
workplace-wrk-29.answersB: Send it because the request came from the client’s real mailbox and the personal address belongs to the same person.
workplace-wrk-29.answersC: Verify the request through a known contact and keep the file inside approved secure channels; escalate if the client’s normal system is unavailable.
workplace-wrk-29.explanation: A real relationship does not make an unapproved data destination safe. Compromised mailboxes and genuine users under pressure can both create risky requests.
workplace-wrk-29.proTip: Trust the relationship; still verify the destination and the data-handling rule.

workplace-wrk-30.title: The assistant’s invite has a login button
workplace-wrk-30.prompt: A familiar executive assistant sends a calendar invite for a rescheduled leadership meeting. The description says “agenda restricted—authenticate to view” and links to a Microsoft-looking sign-in page.
workplace-wrk-30.answersA: Sign in because the invite came from a familiar assistant and restricted agendas are normal.
workplace-wrk-30.answersB: Open the calendar/meeting system directly or ask the assistant through a known channel; do not authenticate through the invite link.
workplace-wrk-30.answersC: Check whether the meeting exists in the normal calendar and whether the organizer address is expected.
workplace-wrk-30.explanation: Compromised calendar accounts can send believable invites. Sensitive-meeting context makes credential prompts feel routine.
workplace-wrk-30.proTip: A meeting invite should not become a new login route.

workplace-wrk-31.title: MFA fatigue at 7:03 a.m.
workplace-wrk-31.prompt: You wake to six MFA prompts for your work account. A Teams message from “IT” says the prompts are part of a security test and asks you to approve the next one to stop the notifications.
workplace-wrk-31.answersA: Deny all prompts, contact IT/security through the official channel, and change credentials if compromise is suspected.
workplace-wrk-31.answersB: Use the account security page to review sessions and revoke unknown access before calling IT.
workplace-wrk-31.answersC: Approve once to stop the prompts, then change the password immediately.
workplace-wrk-31.explanation: MFA fatigue attacks rely on annoyance and timing. Approval gives the access the attacker is repeatedly requesting.
workplace-wrk-31.proTip: Annoyance is a pressure tactic, not proof.

workplace-wrk-32.title: The login page is real; the app is not
workplace-wrk-32.prompt: A link opens a genuine Microsoft/Google login page. After signing in, a third-party app asks for permission to read your mail, files, contacts and calendar “to deliver the document.”
workplace-wrk-32.answersA: Review the publisher and exact permissions with security before granting anything.
workplace-wrk-32.answersB: Approve because the login page is genuine and the provider would block malicious apps.
workplace-wrk-32.answersC: Do not approve; close it and access the document through the company’s approved collaboration tools or verify the app with IT.
workplace-wrk-32.explanation: OAuth abuse can use a real login page and still grant a malicious app persistent access.
workplace-wrk-32.proTip: Authenticate the app, not just the login page.

workplace-wrk-33.title: The break-room QR says “benefits update”
workplace-wrk-33.prompt: A professionally printed QR sticker near the break room says employees must scan to confirm next year’s benefits. The page uses company colors and asks for SSO plus an MFA approval.
workplace-wrk-33.answersA: Use it because the QR is physically inside the office and benefits season is approaching.
workplace-wrk-33.answersB: Do not use the QR; check the HR portal/intranet or ask HR whether the campaign is real.
workplace-wrk-33.answersC: Report the sticker to security and photograph it for investigation without entering credentials.
workplace-wrk-33.explanation: Attackers can place physical QR codes in trusted spaces. Physical proximity does not authenticate a digital destination.
workplace-wrk-33.proTip: Inside the office is not the same as inside the company network.

workplace-wrk-34.title: This extension fixes the broken portal
workplace-wrk-34.prompt: A support article shared in chat says a browser extension fixes a compatibility problem with a critical vendor portal. The extension asks to read and change data on all websites.
workplace-wrk-34.answersA: Verify the extension and fix with IT/security or the vendor’s official documentation before installing it.
workplace-wrk-34.answersB: Use a managed browser or approved workaround until IT validates the extension.
workplace-wrk-34.answersC: Install it because the portal is business-critical and the extension has many positive reviews.
workplace-wrk-34.explanation: Extensions can read sessions, forms and credentials across sites. Popularity and urgency are not sufficient approval.
workplace-wrk-34.proTip: A browser extension can become a silent employee with access to every tab.

workplace-wrk-35.title: “Export your vault for recovery”
workplace-wrk-35.prompt: A message claiming to be from your password-manager provider says a synchronization error could corrupt your vault and asks you to export it to a recovery portal immediately.
workplace-wrk-35.answersA: Back up using the product’s documented local recovery method only after verifying the issue independently.
workplace-wrk-35.answersB: Export the vault but encrypt the file before uploading it to the recovery portal.
workplace-wrk-35.answersC: Do not export the vault; open the password manager directly and contact support through its official site/app.
workplace-wrk-35.explanation: A password vault export is a concentrated copy of your credentials. Encryption does not help if the attacker controls the recovery process or key entry.
workplace-wrk-35.proTip: Your vault is the crown jewels; recovery should never begin from an unsolicited link.

workplace-wrk-36.title: Security asks for your API key
workplace-wrk-36.prompt: Someone in a developer chat says a leaked API key is causing abuse and asks you to paste the current key into a “secret scanner” bot so it can verify whether the leak is real.
workplace-wrk-36.answersA: Paste only the last half of the key so the bot can compare it without receiving the full secret.
workplace-wrk-36.answersB: Do not paste the key; rotate/revoke it through the official secrets platform and follow the security incident process.
workplace-wrk-36.answersC: Notify security and check logs/secret-scanning alerts through trusted tools.
workplace-wrk-36.explanation: Partial secrets can still aid attacks, and a scanner does not need you to disclose the secret to prove it exists.
workplace-wrk-36.proTip: If a secret may be leaked, rotate it—do not redistribute it.

workplace-wrk-37.title: The vendor wants to “show you the fix”
workplace-wrk-37.prompt: A vendor support agent asks you to share your entire screen while you reproduce a billing issue. Your password manager, email and finance apps are open in the background.
workplace-wrk-37.answersA: Share only the specific application/window if approved, close sensitive apps, and verify the support session through the vendor’s official case.
workplace-wrk-37.answersB: Record the issue and provide sanitized screenshots/logs instead of live full-screen access if possible.
workplace-wrk-37.answersC: Share the full screen because you can stop the session if the agent opens anything sensitive.
workplace-wrk-37.explanation: Notifications, autofill prompts and background windows can expose secrets before you react.
workplace-wrk-37.proTip: Screen sharing is data sharing—scope it like any other access.

workplace-wrk-38.title: The CFO is live on video
workplace-wrk-38.prompt: You join a video call where people who look and sound like senior executives discuss a confidential acquisition. They direct you to execute an unusual payment immediately and say written approval will follow.
workplace-wrk-38.answersA: Ask for the normal written approval and a second independent approver before taking action.
workplace-wrk-38.answersB: Proceed because multiple executives are visibly present and the discussion includes confidential company details.
workplace-wrk-38.answersC: Do not rely on the call alone; follow established payment approvals and independently verify with known executives or signatories.
workplace-wrk-38.explanation: Deepfake or synthetic video can reproduce faces and voices, while breached data can supply internal context. Process must authenticate the transaction.
workplace-wrk-38.proTip: Video presence is evidence of pixels, not payment authority.

workplace-wrk-39.title: The conference USB says “speaker materials”
workplace-wrk-39.prompt: After a conference, you find a branded USB drive in your event bag labeled “Speaker Slides + Templates.” Your laptop blocks it and asks whether to allow the device to run setup software.
workplace-wrk-39.answersA: Allow the setup because the USB came inside an official conference bag.
workplace-wrk-39.answersB: Do not run it; obtain materials from the event’s official download site and hand the device to IT/security if required.
workplace-wrk-39.answersC: Open it only on an isolated, security-approved analysis system if your role requires investigation.
workplace-wrk-39.explanation: Physical branding and event context can make removable media feel trustworthy. Unknown devices can carry malware or emulate input devices.
workplace-wrk-39.proTip: Branded plastic is not a trust certificate.

workplace-wrk-40.title: Support wants a recovery token
workplace-wrk-40.prompt: A cloud-support contact says an outage corrupted tenant metadata and asks for an admin recovery token so they can restore service. The case number they quote is real.
workplace-wrk-40.answersA: Do not provide the token; verify the request inside the official support case and use provider-documented recovery procedures with internal security.
workplace-wrk-40.answersB: Escalate to your cloud account team/security contacts and ask for a support method that does not disclose reusable credentials.
workplace-wrk-40.answersC: Provide a short-lived token because the case number is genuine and service restoration is urgent.
workplace-wrk-40.explanation: Real support cases can be hijacked or referenced by attackers. Recovery/admin tokens are high-impact credentials and should remain under customer control.
workplace-wrk-40.proTip: A real case number does not authorize secret transfer.

workplace-wrk-41.title: Register your new MFA device before you're locked out
workplace-wrk-41.prompt: An email says your MFA method is being upgraded and you must register a new device within the hour through the linked form, or lose access to your account today.
workplace-wrk-41.answersA: Go directly to your company's identity portal to check and manage MFA settings instead of the link.
workplace-wrk-41.answersB: Register through the link quickly to avoid losing access.
workplace-wrk-41.answersC: Register through the link, and also share the current MFA code to 'transfer' it.
workplace-wrk-41.explanation: A real MFA change is managed inside your company's own identity system, not through a countdown email that hands you a new device-registration link.
workplace-wrk-41.proTip: MFA changes happen in the identity portal you already use, never in a link that emailed you.

workplace-wrk-42.title: The auditors need this file before they leave at noon
workplace-wrk-42.prompt: An email claiming to be from an external audit firm says a sensitive financial file must be uploaded to a shared link before the auditors leave at noon, or the finding goes down as unresolved.
workplace-wrk-42.answersA: Upload the file quickly to the link to meet the deadline.
workplace-wrk-42.answersB: Confirm the request with your own audit or compliance contact before sending anything.
workplace-wrk-42.answersC: Upload the file, and also send a follow-up file they ask for afterward.
workplace-wrk-42.explanation: Real audit requests go through an established engagement contact and process; a same-day external deadline attached to a random shared link is a hallmark of a pretext for data theft.
workplace-wrk-42.proTip: A deadline set by the email itself is not a reason to skip verifying who's asking.

workplace-wrk-43.title: HR portal: confirm your bank details for pay
workplace-wrk-43.prompt: An email styled like your HR system says your payroll bank details need re-confirmation before this month's pay run, with a link to a form that asks for your account and routing numbers.
workplace-wrk-43.answersA: Log into your real HR/payroll system directly instead of using the emailed link.
workplace-wrk-43.answersB: Fill in the form, and also update it again when a follow-up email asks.
workplace-wrk-43.answersC: Fill in the form through the link to make sure you're paid on time.
workplace-wrk-43.explanation: Payroll bank-detail changes are one of the most common employee-targeted business email compromises, because a missed paycheck is a powerful, personal pressure point.
workplace-wrk-43.proTip: Pay details are updated inside the payroll system you already use, not through an emailed form.

workplace-wrk-44.title: Data subject request: send everything on this person
workplace-wrk-44.prompt: An email citing data-protection law demands your team send everything held about a named individual within 48 hours, with no verification of identity or authority attached.
workplace-wrk-44.answersA: Compile and send the requested data quickly to comply with the law.
workplace-wrk-44.answersB: Route the request through your organization's official data-protection process before sending anything.
workplace-wrk-44.answersC: Send a partial file quickly and promise the rest later.
workplace-wrk-44.explanation: Legitimate data-subject requests go through a verified intake process precisely because unverified requests are a known vector for extracting sensitive personal data.
workplace-wrk-44.proTip: A legal-sounding deadline doesn't replace your organization's real verification process.

workplace-wrk-45.title: A candidate sent their portfolio
workplace-wrk-45.prompt: A promising candidate for an open role emails their portfolio as an attached file, with a note asking you to enable editing to see the full formatting.
workplace-wrk-45.answersA: Open it and enable editing since they seem like a strong candidate.
workplace-wrk-45.answersB: Open it, enable editing, and forward it to the rest of the hiring panel.
workplace-wrk-45.answersC: Open it in a preview or protected view without enabling editing, or ask for a link to a standard hosting service instead.
workplace-wrk-45.explanation: Malicious documents targeting hiring managers routinely arrive as convincing candidate portfolios, and the 'enable editing' prompt is the exact step that activates the payload.
workplace-wrk-45.proTip: A request to 'enable editing' to see formatting is not something a real document needs.

workplace-wrk-46.title: The meeting bot is already in the call
workplace-wrk-46.prompt: An AI note-taking bot joins your confidential client call uninvited, asking to be admitted so it can share the transcript and recording with 'the organizer' afterward.
workplace-wrk-46.answersA: Admit it, since these bots are common in meetings now.
workplace-wrk-46.answersB: Remove it and confirm with the actual organizer whether they added a note-taker before continuing.
workplace-wrk-46.answersC: Admit it, and continue the meeting without mentioning it to anyone.
workplace-wrk-46.explanation: An uninvited AI meeting bot can silently record and export a confidential conversation to an outside party; its presence should be confirmed with the meeting organizer, not assumed.
workplace-wrk-46.proTip: Anything that can record the whole meeting deserves the same check as any other uninvited guest.

workplace-wrk-47.title: Facilities: renew your badge details here
workplace-wrk-47.prompt: An email styled like Facilities says your access badge is expiring and asks you to confirm your employee ID and a photo of your badge on a linked renewal site to avoid being locked out of the building.
workplace-wrk-47.answersA: Confirm the details on the site to avoid losing building access.
workplace-wrk-47.answersB: Confirm the details, and also photograph your badge as asked.
workplace-wrk-47.answersC: Check badge renewal directly with Facilities or Security in person or through a known internal system.
workplace-wrk-47.explanation: Physical access-credential phishing collects exactly what's needed to clone a badge or impersonate an employee at the door, dressed up as routine building admin.
workplace-wrk-47.proTip: Badge and access changes go through Facilities or Security directly, not a link that emailed you.

workplace-wrk-48.title: Security is calling - read back your code
workplace-wrk-48.prompt: Someone calling from the 'security team' says they're verifying a suspicious login on your account and asks you to read back the 6-digit code that just arrived by text so they can confirm it's really you.
workplace-wrk-48.answersA: Read the code back since they say it's just to verify you.
workplace-wrk-48.answersB: Read the code back, and also confirm your password to speed up the process.
workplace-wrk-48.answersC: Don't share the code; hang up and contact IT/Security through a known internal number to check.
workplace-wrk-48.explanation: A verification code sent to you is meant to stay with you - reading it to a caller hands them exactly what they need to complete their own login as you.
workplace-wrk-48.proTip: A code sent to you verifies you, not the person asking you to read it out loud.
